claim: Purpose is the preset a director sets before touching anything else: it decides how big the subject sits in the frame and what the frame is actually about. Reach for it when you want the shot to do a job - plant the location, land a face, hold a beat - instead of hand-dialling size, lens and duration one at a time.

options.clause: wide shot, scenery, full body, distant subject
backlighting, emerging from shadow, dramatic entrance
close-up, wide-eyed, surprised
dynamic pose, motion blur, running
upper body, open mouth, talking
blurry, motion blur, out of focus
extreme close-up, cropped, object focus
medium shot, standing, expressionless
atmospheric, ambient light, looking away
close-up, soccer ball, object focus

review.issue: detail ("extreme close-up, cropped, object focus") and insert ("close-up, soccer ball, object focus") share the same tag core, and in a soccer scene the detail panel will almost certainly land on the ball too — two options, one picture. reveal ("emerging from shadow, dramatic entrance") and mood ("atmospheric, ambient light") are description rather than danbooru tags: none of those four phrases are trained, so those panels rest entirely on "backlighting" and "looking away".
review.fix: Anchor detail on something else the subject sentence already contains — "extreme close-up, jersey number, fabric texture" — and let insert own the ball. Rewrite reveal as "backlighting, silhouette, rim lighting" and mood as "dark, dramatic shadow, looking away", which are all trained tags.

claim: Framing type declares how many bodies are in frame and whose vantage we borrow, which rewrites the entire tag stack underneath it. It is the difference between a portrait, a conversation and a shot where the character is not the subject at all.

options.clause: solo focus, one person in frame
2boys, multiple boys
3boys, multiple boys
multiple boys, 6+boys, team lineup
over the shoulder, 2boys, blurry foreground shoulder
pov, first-person view, pov hands
upper body, wide-eyed, open mouth
no humans, object focus, close-up
no humans, empty, scenery only
crowd focus, many people, spectators fill frame

review.issue: Six of ten options directly contradict the fixed subject sentence, which hard-pins "1boy, solo". two_shot/three_shot/group/over_shoulder push 2boys / 3boys / multiple boys / 6+boys against "solo"; insert_object and empty_frame push "no humans" against "1boy, solo, male focus". Animagine weights the subject tags first, so those panels come back as the same lone boy (or with mangled duplicate anatomy) and the card teaches nothing about the value it exists to show. single ("solo focus, one person in frame") also just restates "solo", and crowd restates the "crowd" tag already in the subject. "one person in frame" and "spectators fill frame" are prose, not tags.
review.fix: This variable rewrites the subject's character count, which the identical-subject-sentence method forbids. Either mark renderable:false with that as the skip_reason, or declare an explicit documented subject exception for this card only (drop "solo" and the count tag from the fixed sentence) rather than shipping clauses that silently lose to the subject. If it stays, give single an empty clause (it is the baseline) and rewrite crowd so it adds foreground crowd occlusion rather than restating "crowd".

claim: Keyframe mode decides whether the shot is a single still driven into motion by i2v or an interpolation between two or three authored frames. Reach for start_end when the shot has to arrive somewhere specific, and start_mid_end when the middle of the move is the point.
skip_reason: The variable is about how many authored frames feed the video pass and what happens between them. A still is by definition one frame, so all three values produce the identical panel.

claim: Priority is the shot's claim on the budget: it tells trimmers and allocators which shots to sacrifice first when the runtime or the render bill does not fit. Mark the two shots the film cannot survive without as critical and let filler absorb the cuts.
skip_reason: Pure scheduling and budget metadata. It changes render allocation and trim order, never a pixel of the image, so four identical panels is the honest result.

claim: Match_prev asks this shot's cut to land on something the previous shot already established - the same composition, the same gesture mid-flight, the same eyeline, the same light. It is how a cut feels authored rather than merely next.
skip_reason: Every value describes a relationship to a different shot. One still has no previous frame to match, so nothing in the panel can express the option; you would need a two-panel pair, which breaks the one-render-per-option method.

claim: Facing is which way the body is turned, independent of where the camera sits or where the eyes go. It is the first thing a viewer reads off a character: to_camera confronts, three-quarter is the workhorse of conversation, and back withholds the face entirely.

options.clause: facing viewer, front view, body facing forward
three-quarter view, body turned left
three-quarter view, body turned right
profile, from side, facing left
profile, from side, facing right
from behind, three-quarter view, shoulder toward viewer
from behind, facing away, back turned

review.issue: Danbooru/Animagine has no reliable lateral vocabulary: "body turned left", "facing left", "facing right" are not trained tags, and the model mirrors at random. three_quarter_left vs three_quarter_right and profile_left vs profile_right will come back as two arbitrary pairs — four options, two pictures. back and back_three_quarter are both dominated by "from behind" and will read the same; "shoulder toward viewer" carries no weight against it.
review.fix: Use the tags that exist — "facing viewer", "profile" / "from side", "from behind", "facing away" — and either collapse each L/R pair into one option or keep them while stating in the claim that direction is a coin flip this model will not honour. Give back_three_quarter a real separator such as "looking back" or "looking over shoulder".

claim: Camera height is where the lens physically lives, authored separately from whether it tilts. Dropping to knee or ground makes the world tower and the figure heroic even with a level lens; lifting to overhead or aerial turns a person into a marker on a map.

options.clause: ground level, camera on the ground
ankle height camera, very low viewpoint
knee height camera, low viewpoint
waist height camera, slightly low viewpoint
chest height camera
eye level, straight-on
high viewpoint, elevated camera
overhead view, directly above
aerial view, far above, distant ground

review.issue: "ankle height camera", "knee height camera", "waist height camera" and "chest height camera" are invented phrases with no danbooru training behind them; the only signal Animagine reads in those clauses is "low viewpoint" ≈ "from below". ground/ankle/knee/waist therefore collapse toward one low-angle panel and chest/eye toward the baseline — nine options for roughly four pictures. The card also overlaps shot.cam.angle wholesale: height.high/overhead/aerial and angle.high/birds_eye/top_down all resolve through the same "from above" token, so the claim that height is authored independently of tilt is not expressible in this model.
review.fix: Cut to values the vocabulary supports — ground / low / eye / high / overhead — using real tags ("from below", "eye level", "from above", "directly from above"). Then either merge this card into shot.cam.angle or state in the claim that in the still pass height and angle share one control, and let the card demonstrate only the extremes.

claim: Angle is the classic dominance lever: the tilt of the lens relative to the subject. Low makes a figure monumental, high makes them small and observed, and dutch says the world itself is off its axis.

options.clause: straight-on, eye level, level horizon
from below, low angle
from above, high angle
bird's-eye view, from far above
worm's-eye view, extreme low angle, from below
top-down view, from directly above
dutch angle, tilted horizon

review.issue: birds_eye ("bird's-eye view, from far above") and top_down ("top-down view, from directly above") are the same instruction in two phrasings and will render as one picture; both also duplicate cam.height.overhead/aerial. worms_eye ("worm's-eye view, extreme low angle, from below") differs from low ("from below, low angle") only by intensifiers the model largely ignores.
review.fix: Keep level / low / high / dutch as the load-bearing four plus one overhead extreme, and delete the twin. Assign overhead ownership to exactly one card (angle or height, not both).

claim: The core motion verb of the shot - what the camera does across its duration, from a locked static to a whip pan. It is the single loudest choice in a moving shot and the one directors name first.
skip_reason: All twenty values describe motion over time. A still cannot separate push from zoom_in, pan_l from pan_r, or orbit from dolly; at best every panel picks up generic motion blur and the card teaches nothing.

claim: Move speed separates how fast from what direction, so one move verb serves both a whispered push and a chase. The same dolly at crawl is dread and at whip is panic.
skip_reason: A rate of change per second. With no second frame there is no rate, and the six values collapse into one identical still.

claim: Easing is what separates an operated camera from a machine-made one - linear motion is the single clearest tell that nobody was holding the rig. Snap and overshoot make a move feel physical; settle makes it feel like someone found the frame.
skip_reason: Pure timing curve. It describes acceleration inside a move that a still image does not contain.

claim: Anchor is the point a move converges on: a push into the centre of the frame and a push into a character's eye are two different shots with the same verb. Set it to face when the move is about a person and to horizon when it is about the world.
skip_reason: An anchor only exists while the camera is moving - it names the fixed point of a transform. Without a move there is nothing for it to anchor, and any still version would just be duplicating shot.comp.thirds_bias.

claim: Rig is the baseline motion texture a sequence inherits, so individual shots need not each dial in shake. Locked reads as observation and control; handheld_heavy and shoulder read as being inside the event with somebody breathing.
skip_reason: Rig expresses itself entirely as how the frame drifts, breathes or jolts over time. Frozen on one frame, locked and handheld_heavy are indistinguishable.

claim: Frequency is what gives a shake its character - amplitude alone makes every disturbance feel the same. Breath is a held human presence, walk and run are footfall, impact is a single hit and rumble is the ground itself.
skip_reason: A frequency is cycles per second. One frame samples the waveform at a single instant, so all six values land on the same picture.

claim: Zoom kind documents whether a zoom is faked in post by cropping pixels or sold as an optical change - which is the whole reason renders are made oversized. Digital_crop is free and costs resolution; optical_feel costs overscan and keeps detail.
skip_reason: A render-pipeline bookkeeping flag about crop versus overscan during a zoom. It has no still-frame signature and only two values, neither of which changes what the generator draws.

claim: Shutter angle is how crisp or smeared motion reads - 45 gives you the strobed, glassy sharpness of a war film, 360 gives you the smeared drift of a dream. It is the cheapest way to change how violent or how liquid movement feels without changing the movement.
skip_reason: It governs how much motion is integrated per exposure, so it only shows up when the subject or camera is moving. The fixed subject sentence is a standing figure, and Animagine has a single blunt motion blur tag rather than five gradable steps.

claim: Lens look lets an author state the feel without knowing millimetres, and it changes the geometry of the subject rather than just the crop. Wide bends and separates, tele flattens and stacks the crowd right onto the shoulders, macro abandons the person for a texture.

options.clause: ultra wide angle, exaggerated perspective, stretched edges
wide angle lens, strong perspective
natural perspective, undistorted
portrait lens, 85mm, mild compression
telephoto lens, compressed perspective
super telephoto, extreme compression, long lens
fisheye lens, fisheye, barrel distortion
anamorphic lens, anamorphic widescreen
macro lens, extreme close-up, macro photography

review.issue: portrait ("portrait lens, 85mm, mild compression"), tele and super_tele all resolve to the single telephoto look the model knows — millimetre numbers are inert tokens in Animagine — so three options land on one panel. macro smuggles two other variables: "extreme close-up" is framing already owned by shot.purpose.detail, and "macro photography" pulls the render toward photoreal and off the anime style the whole system depends on. anamorphic's "anamorphic widescreen" tends to draw letterbox bars, which is shot.frame.letterbox's job.
review.fix: Collapse portrait/tele/super_tele into one "telephoto compression" option. Rewrite macro as "macro, extreme close-up detail" without the word photography. Drop "widescreen" from anamorphic and let it ride on "anamorphic lens" alone (or express it via the flare/bokeh cards, which already carry the anamorphic look).

claim: Compression is how flat the background stacks behind the subject, addressable on its own when focal length alone is not selling it. Expanded pushes the stadium away and isolates the figure; hyper_compressed glues the crowd to his back so he cannot escape it.

options.clause: wide angle distortion, exaggerated depth, receding background
natural perspective, neutral depth
telephoto compression, flattened background
extreme telephoto compression, flat stacked background, long lens look

review.issue: The whole card re-renders shot.lens.look. expanded ("wide angle distortion, exaggerated depth") ≈ look.ultra_wide/wide ("ultra wide angle, exaggerated perspective"); compressed ("telephoto compression, flattened background") ≈ look.tele ("telephoto lens, compressed perspective"); hyper_compressed ≈ look.super_tele. Internally, compressed and hyper_compressed differ only by intensifiers — Animagine has one tele look, not a gradable compression axis — so those two are one panel. natural is the baseline.
review.fix: Mark renderable:false with skip_reason "no vocabulary separable from focal length in the still pass; the axis is already shown by shot.lens.look", or reduce to two panels (natural, compressed) and rewrite the claim so it does not promise a control the model cannot separate from lens.look.

claim: Distortion is the deliberate bulge or pinch of the frame's straight lines, and in anime it is a device rather than a defect. Strong_barrel and fisheye are what a panic beat or a comedy blow-up look like from the inside.

options.clause: rectilinear, straight lines, no distortion
slight barrel distortion, gently curved edges
strong barrel distortion, bulging center, curved lines
fisheye, fisheye lens, circular distortion
pincushion distortion, inward curving edges

review.issue: fisheye duplicates lens.look.fisheye and comp.perspective.fisheye across cards. mild_barrel ("slight barrel distortion, gently curved edges") is an intensity step below strong_barrel that the model does not grade, so it will read as none. pincushion has almost no representation in this model and will likely be a third copy of the none panel.
review.fix: Own fisheye here and remove it from lens.look and comp.perspective. Drop mild_barrel, or replace the pair with one barrel option plus fisheye as the extreme. Keep pincushion only if you are prepared for it to be the card's null result — and say so in the claim rather than after the render.

claim: Flare is the mood signature authors reach for constantly, and under floodlights it is nearly free. Starburst says hard and clean, warm_bloom says nostalgic, veiling says the light is in your eyes and you cannot see properly.

options.clause: no lens flare, clean image
subtle lens flare, small flare
anamorphic lens flare, horizontal blue streak
warm bloom, glowing haze, soft glow
starburst, sun star, pointed light rays
veiling glare, washed out haze, lifted blacks

claim: The shape of an out-of-focus highlight is most of a night film's identity - a stadium behind a shallow lens is nothing but bokeh. Hexagonal reads mechanical and period, oval_anamorphic reads expensive, swirly reads unstable and antique.

options.clause: circular bokeh, round bokeh, bokeh
hexagonal bokeh, six-sided highlights
oval bokeh, anamorphic bokeh, stretched highlights
swirly bokeh, spiraling background blur
cat's eye bokeh, clipped highlights at frame edges
bloom, glowing orbs, soft light blobs

review.issue: Aperture-blade shape is not in the danbooru vocabulary. Animagine has one "bokeh" concept, so hexagonal, oval_anamorphic and cats_eye will most likely all render as ordinary round highlights — six options for roughly three looks (generic bokeh / swirly / bloom). Compounding it, the fixed subject sentence contains no shallow-DOF cue, so any panel whose clause does not itself say "blurry background" may have no bokeh at all to shape. bloom_blobs also duplicates lens.flare.warm_bloom and fx.glow.
review.fix: Put an identical DOF anchor in every clause ("blurry background, bokeh" in all six — constant across panels, so the method still holds), and cut the card to the shapes the model can draw: circular, swirly, oval_anamorphic, plus bloom_blobs only if flare.warm_bloom is dropped.

claim: Diffusion is the cheapest way to make twenty separately generated shots feel like one film, which is why it should be set high in the hierarchy and inherited. Pro_mist lifts the blacks and haloes every floodlight; heavy_diffusion turns the whole frame into a memory.

options.clause: clean lens, crisp contrast, no diffusion
light diffusion filter, gentle halo on highlights
pro-mist filter, misty halation, lifted blacks
heavy diffusion, dreamy soft focus, blooming highlights
glimmer filter, sparkling highlights, twinkle
smoked glass filter, hazy, muted contrast

review.issue: none is baseline plus a negation, and light_diffusion ("light diffusion filter, gentle halo on highlights") is a weaker phrasing of pro_mist ("pro-mist filter, misty halation, lifted blacks"); smoke_glass ("hazy, muted contrast") sits on the same haze axis. Six options, probably three separable looks.
review.fix: none → empty clause; merge light_diffusion into pro_mist; keep heavy_diffusion as the extreme and glimmer as the genuine outlier ("sparkle" is a strong trained anime tag, so that panel really will diverge); keep smoke_glass only if it drops "hazy" and leans on "muted contrast, desaturated".

claim: Depth of field is the fastest character-from-background separation there is, and it decides whether the world is a place or a texture. Deep keeps the stadium a fact; very_shallow deletes it and leaves only a boy and some coloured light.

options.clause: deep focus, everything in focus, sharp background
moderate depth of field, slightly soft background
depth of field, blurry background, bokeh
extremely shallow depth of field, heavily blurred background, bokeh
split diopter, foreground and background both sharp, split focus

review.issue: medium ("moderate depth of field, slightly soft background") sits between the two states Animagine actually has — "deep focus" and "blurry background" — and will not separate from deep. split_diopter has essentially no representation in the model and will most likely come back as ordinary deep focus, a second copy of the deep panel.
review.fix: Reduce to deep / shallow / very_shallow. Keep split_diopter only with an explicit note in the card that it is the one value the still pass is expected to miss (it is really an ffmpeg/composite job), or mark it as a per-option skip.

claim: Focus point names what must be sharp so the generator and the blur pass agree on what the shot is about. Setting it to hands or prop is how you make a shot about an object while a person is still standing in it.

options.clause: focus on eyes, sharp eyes
focus on face, sharp face, soft background
subject in focus, blurry background
focus on hands, sharp hands, hand in foreground
focus on object, sharp prop, blurry person
foreground in focus, blurry midground, blurry background
midground in focus, blurry foreground, blurry background
background in focus, out of focus subject, blurry foreground
hyperfocal, everything sharp, deep focus

review.issue: hyperfocal ("hyperfocal, everything sharp, deep focus") is the same instruction as shot.focus.dof.deep ("deep focus, everything in focus, sharp background") — two cards, one panel. subject ("subject in focus, blurry background") likewise duplicates dof.shallow ("depth of field, blurry background, bokeh"). Within the card, eyes / face / subject will not separate because the fixed subject sentence frames a whole figure in a stadium, not a close-up. prop asks for a "sharp prop" when the subject sentence contains no prop, so the model invents one and the panel changes more than the option.
review.fix: Delete hyperfocal (owned by dof) and merge eyes into face, or state in the claim that this card only reads at close-up scale. Name a scene-native object in prop: "focus on soccer ball, blurry person", and use that same object anywhere else a prop is needed.

claim: Behavior is what focus does across the shot rather than where it starts - a rack is a dramatic beat, a reveal performed with the lens instead of a cut. Snap_focus lands attention like a slap; soft_throughout refuses to let the audience settle.
skip_reason: Five of the six values are transitions between two focus states over time. Only soft_throughout is static, and it is already covered by shot.focus.dof, so a still card would show one usable panel and five duplicates of shot.focus.point.

claim: Where a character looks carries the emotional read and is what stitches a reverse-shot pair together. Into_lens breaks the fourth wall and confronts the audience; off_left throws attention at something we have not been shown yet; closed shuts us out entirely.

options.clause: looking at viewer, eye contact
looking to the side, eyes turned left
looking to the side, eyes turned right
looking up
looking down
looking off-screen to the left, looking away, gaze past frame edge
looking off-screen to the right, looking away, gaze past frame edge
closed eyes
looking at object, gaze fixed on prop

review.issue: left ("looking to the side, eyes turned left") and right differ only by a word the model has no tag for, and off_left/off_right stack "looking away" on top of that same non-tag. All four carry one instruction — "looking to the side / looking away" — so four options produce one or two pictures. at_object ("looking at object, gaze fixed on prop") points at a prop the fixed subject sentence does not contain, so the model must invent one and the panel changes more than the option.
review.fix: Reduce to the trained set: into_lens "looking at viewer, eye contact", to_side "looking to the side", away "looking away", up "looking up", down "looking down", closed "closed eyes". If L/R values must survive the enum, say in the claim that the still pass cannot fix the side. Point at_object at an object the scene already owns: "looking at soccer ball".

claim: Screen direction keeps travel and chase geometry consistent so a runner does not silently reverse himself between cuts. Set it once for a sequence and every shot in the pursuit agrees which way the goal is.

options.clause: moving to the right, running to the right
moving to the left, running to the left
running toward viewer, approaching camera, foreshortening
running away from viewer, receding into the distance
standing still, no movement

review.issue: l_to_r and r_to_l hit the same missing left/right vocabulary and will mirror at random. Separately, every clause injects "running" or "moving", a pose the option does not own and which shot.purpose.action already teaches — the panels will read as "the subject is now running" as much as as direction. static's "no movement" is a negation.
review.fix: Keep to_camera and away_from_camera, which do work ("facing viewer" / "from behind" are trained tags), fold the lateral pair into one "moving across frame, profile" option or accept the coin flip explicitly, and give static an empty clause.

claim: Balance is the distribution of visual weight, and it is what an author actually means when they say a frame feels wrong but cannot say why. Symmetrical is formal and inhuman, weighted_top crushes the subject, chaotic is what a frame looks like when nothing is under control.

options.clause: symmetrical composition, mirrored framing, centered
subject on the left, empty space on the right
subject on the right, empty space on the left
visual weight at the bottom, heavy lower frame, empty upper frame
visual weight at the top, heavy upper frame, empty lower frame
diagonal composition, elements arranged along a diagonal
radial composition, elements radiating from the center
chaotic composition, unbalanced, cluttered frame

review.issue: weighted_bottom, weighted_top and radial are written in critic's language, not tags — "visual weight at the bottom", "heavy lower frame", "empty upper frame" have no danbooru counterpart and will read as baseline. asym_left/asym_right restate thirds_bias.left_third/right_third and hit the left/right gap. symmetrical duplicates thirds_bias.symmetrical, and radial ("radial composition, elements radiating from the center") duplicates comp.leading_lines.radial ("radial lines, lines radiating from the center") almost word for word.
review.fix: Delete the values other cards already own (asym_*, symmetrical, radial) and express the weighting values as content the model can actually draw — e.g. weighted_top as "towering structure above, small figure below", weighted_bottom as "low horizon, open sky above" — or drop them. What is left that is genuinely this card's own is diagonal and chaotic.

claim: Lateral placement is the composition choice authors want most often and can least easily describe. Centre is confrontational and static, a third is conversational and open, and edge is a frame that is already halfway to losing him.

options.clause: centered composition, subject in the middle
rule of thirds, subject on the left third
rule of thirds, subject on the right third
golden ratio composition, subject left of center
golden ratio composition, subject right of center
perfectly symmetrical, dead center, mirrored
subject at the left edge, cropped at frame left
subject at the right edge, cropped at frame right

review.issue: Eight options, at most three distinguishable pictures. golden_l ("subject left of center") is the same instruction as left_third ("subject on the left third") — Animagine does not resolve golden ratio versus rule of thirds. symmetrical ("perfectly symmetrical, dead center, mirrored") is the same as center and also duplicates shot.comp.balance.symmetrical in another card. edge_left/edge_right hit the same left/right gap as facing and eyeline.
review.fix: Cut to center / off_center / edge (keeping L/R only if you accept the mirror flip and say so), delete golden_l and golden_r, and let shot.comp.balance own symmetry so the two cards do not ship the same panel.

claim: Headroom is simultaneously the most common framing mistake and the most common deliberate tension device. Tight presses a character against the top of the frame and makes the space feel too small for him; loose strands him at the bottom of an empty sky.

options.clause: tight headroom, head near top of frame
normal headroom, balanced space above head
loose headroom, large empty space above head
head out of frame, cropped head, top of head cut off

review.issue: "tight headroom" and "normal headroom" are not trained phrases — danbooru expresses headroom only through shot-size and crop tags — so tight and normal are likely to be the same picture, and normal is the baseline anyway. cropped_top is the one value with real vocabulary behind it ("head out of frame").
review.fix: Give normal an empty clause, keep tight / loose / cropped_top, and lean on the crop tags the model knows: tight "head near top edge, cropped at top" is weak but survivable, loose "large empty space above head, small figure" is the one worth authoring carefully.

claim: Lookroom is the space in front of a character's gaze, and its absence is instantly claustrophobic. Give him room and the frame is balanced and forward-looking; take it away and he is pressed into the edge of his own shot.

options.clause: balanced lookroom, open space in front of the gaze
empty space at frame left, subject on the right
empty space at frame right, subject on the left
equal space on both sides, centered subject
no lookroom, face pressed against the frame edge

review.issue: Lookroom is space in front of a gaze, and the fixed subject sentence sets no gaze. With no eyeline in the panel, "empty space at frame left, subject on the right" is nothing but lateral placement — i.e. shot.comp.thirds_bias again, with the same unreliable left/right vocabulary. auto ("balanced lookroom, open space in front of the gaze") is prose about the concept rather than anything the model can draw, and none is a negation.
review.fix: Honest call is renderable:false: the option is only legible relative to an eyeline the fixed subject does not fix, and once you add one you are rendering shot.comp.eyeline. If it stays renderable, pin one identical gaze tag ("looking to the side") in every clause of this card and state in the claim that the panels will look like thirds_bias.

claim: Horizon placement decides whether a character dominates the sky or is crushed under the weight of the ground. Low horizon makes him a monument against open air; high horizon buries him in the pitch.

options.clause: no horizon visible, no sky in frame
very low horizon line, sky fills most of the frame
horizon on the lower third, sky above
horizon line through the center of the frame
horizon on the upper third, ground fills the lower frame
very high horizon line, ground fills most of the frame

review.issue: low ("very low horizon line, sky fills most of the frame") and lower_third ("horizon on the lower third, sky above") are the same instruction, as are high and upper_third — six options for about four pictures. And the fixed subject sentence puts the camera inside a floodlit stadium bowl surrounded by crowd, where the model rarely draws a horizon at all, so several panels risk silently becoming the none panel.
review.fix: Collapse to none / low / center / high. Note in the claim that the stadium location suppresses this variable, since that constraint is a property of the fixed subject sentence and worth stating before anyone reads the panels.

claim: Leading lines tell the eye where to go, and anime backgrounds lean on them harder than live action ever does. Converging_rails and one_point pull attention down a corridor to the subject; radial detonates outward from him.

options.clause: no leading lines, flat arrangement
one-point perspective, lines converging on a single vanishing point
strong diagonal lines, diagonal leading lines
radial lines, lines radiating from the center
strong vertical lines, tall parallel lines
strong horizontal lines, stacked bands
spiral composition, curving sweeping lines
converging parallel lines, receding rails, strong perspective lines

review.issue: one_point ("one-point perspective, lines converging on a single vanishing point") and converging_rails ("converging parallel lines, receding rails, strong perspective lines") are the same instruction — one card, two identical panels. one_point is additionally a near-verbatim duplicate of shot.comp.perspective.one_point ("one-point perspective, single vanishing point") in another card, and radial duplicates comp.balance.radial.
review.fix: Decide once whether perspective construction belongs to leading_lines or to comp.perspective and delete it from the other. Keep converging_rails only if it names a real line source in the scene ("receding rows of stadium seats"), otherwise drop it. Drop radial from one of the two cards that carry it.

claim: Perspective construction is an explicit background-art decision in anime, made by a person at a drawing board rather than fallen out of a lens. Flat and isometric read as designed and unreal; three_point looms and makes architecture threatening.

options.clause: flat perspective, no vanishing point, orthographic
one-point perspective, single vanishing point
two-point perspective, two vanishing points
three-point perspective, vertical vanishing point, dramatic perspective
isometric view, isometric perspective, parallel projection
fisheye perspective, curved wide angle view
overhead plan view, top-down map view, from directly above

review.issue: fisheye is the third card carrying a fisheye option — lens.look.fisheye ("fisheye lens, fisheye, barrel distortion"), lens.distortion.fisheye ("fisheye, fisheye lens, circular distortion"), and this one — with effectively the same tags, so three cards would ship the same panel. overhead_map ("overhead plan view, top-down map view, from directly above") is the same instruction as cam.angle.top_down and cam.height.overhead. flat's "no vanishing point" is a negation. two_point vs one_point is a distinction Animagine draws only by accident.
review.fix: Give fisheye a single owner (lens.distortion is the natural one) and remove it from the other two cards; likewise give the straight-down view a single owner (cam.angle). Reduce this card to flat / one_point / three_point / isometric — the four the model actually differentiates — and rewrite flat affirmatively as "orthographic, flat composition".

claim: Putting a character inside an in-world aperture states confinement, surveillance or distance in one move and without a line of dialogue. Doorway and fence say we are watching him from outside something; mirror says we are seeing a version of him rather than him.

options.clause: unobstructed view, open frame
framed by a doorway, seen through a door
seen through a window, window frame in the foreground
reflection in a mirror, seen in a mirror, mirror frame
framed by leaves, foliage in the foreground, branches at the edges
framed by silhouetted heads, blurry people in the foreground
framed by curtains, curtain in the foreground
seen through a tunnel mouth, dark tunnel edges
seen through a chain-link fence, fence in the foreground

review.issue: doorway, window, mirror, foliage and curtain are objects a floodlit soccer stadium does not contain. Animagine will honour the aperture by relocating the scene, so those panels change the location as well as the framing device — the option clause ends up rewriting the subject even though it never restates it in text.
review.fix: Prefer apertures the location can supply: "seen through a chain-link fence", "seen through the tunnel mouth, dark edges", "framed by goal netting", "framed by silhouetted heads in the foreground". Drop curtain, foliage and mirror, or move this card to a scene that contains them.

claim: Depth stack states how many distinct planes the frame is built from, and it is the contract the layer variables read. Flat is a poster, three_plane is a shot you can move a camera through, deep_stack is what makes a generated image stop looking like a painting of a place.

options.clause: flat composition, single plane, no depth
two depth planes, subject against background
foreground, midground and background, three depth planes
many overlapping depth layers, deep receding planes

review.issue: "two depth planes", "three depth planes", "foreground, midground and background", "many overlapping depth layers" is meta-language about the composition rather than content the model can draw; Animagine cannot count planes. two_plane, three_plane and deep_stack will land on the same picture, and only flat is likely to separate.
review.fix: State the planes as objects: two_plane "subject against blurred background"; three_plane "blurry foreground silhouette, blurred crowd behind"; deep_stack "layered crowd, receding rows of seats, distant floodlights". That is still only about depth, but it is content the model can stack.

claim: Aspect override lets one shot break ratio without restructuring the chapter around it - a sudden 2.39 insert or a 9:16 phone screen inside a 16:9 film. Reach for it when the shape of the frame is itself the point.
skip_reason: Aspect is the latent canvas geometry, set outside the prompt entirely. There is no tag for it, and changing the render dimensions means the fixed seed no longer holds the composition, which breaks the identical-seed method the card depends on.

claim: Letterbox is aspect change used as a dramatic device rather than a delivery format - bars sliding in to say this moment is bigger than the rest of the film. Dynamic_widen is the version that performs the change on screen.
skip_reason: Bars are a composite drawn over the finished frame in ffmpeg, not something the generator produces. Animagine cannot be asked for a 2.39 bar as distinct from a 2:1 bar, and dynamic_widen is an animated change with no single-frame state.

claim: Caption safe reserves the strip that burnt-in subtitles will occupy so a composition survives delivery instead of putting a face behind the text. Move it to top when the story lives in the lower frame.
skip_reason: An invisible reserved region that constrains where other elements may be placed. It draws nothing itself, so every panel would be identical unless the card faked a caption that is not part of the render.

claim: Direct access to the native post-fx set, appended as it travels down the hierarchy so a scene-level glow and a shot-level flash both survive. Six of the nine have a real single-frame look; punch, shake and ramp are timing operations and get no clause.

options.clause: chromatic aberration, color fringing
glowing, bloom, soft glow
bright white flash, blinding light
overexposed, blown highlights, clipped whites
motion blur, smeared motion
whiteout, white screen, blinding white

review.issue: The card is renderable:true but punch, shake and ramp carry empty clauses. Three of the nine panels will therefore be the unmodified baseline and identical to each other, with no machine-readable reason attached — everywhere else in this set "cannot be shown" is expressed as renderable:false + skip_reason. Separately, flash ("bright white flash, blinding light") and whiteout ("whiteout, white screen, blinding white") are the same instruction, and hot ("overexposed, blown highlights, clipped whites") sits on the same blow-out axis: three options, probably one or two pictures.
review.fix: Add a per-option renderable:false + skip_reason for punch/shake/ramp ("timing operation, no single-frame state") so the schema is honest at option level, and either merge flash into whiteout or scope hot to a partial blow-out ("overexposed, blown highlights" with the frame still legible) versus whiteout as the fully white frame.

claim: The one-frame graphic hit is a defining anime action beat - a single drawing that violates the film's own rendering rules for a sixteenth of a second. Sketch_frame exposes the raw genga underneath; negative and silhouette_pop reduce the character to pure shape at the moment of contact.

options.clause: normal rendering, no impact effect
white flash frame, blown out white, high contrast
black flash frame, blacked out, high contrast
inverted colors, negative image, color inversion
rough sketch, genga, pencil lines, unfinished drawing
silhouette, solid black figure, flat color background

review.issue: The "none" clause "normal rendering, no impact effect" is prose plus a negation. "normal rendering" is not a tag and the negation is ignored, so the baseline panel is being perturbed for no reason.
review.fix: Empty clause.

claim: Drawn motion overlays are native anime language with no photographic equivalent, and they carry force that actual movement cannot. Radial says the camera is being rushed; impact says something just landed; motion_trail says he is already gone.

options.clause: no speed lines, clean background
radial speed lines, emphasis lines radiating from the center
horizontal speed lines, sideways motion lines
vertical speed lines, downward motion lines
impact lines, emphasis lines, burst lines
motion trail, afterimage, trailing streaks

review.issue: The "none" clause is "no speed lines, clean background". Negation does nothing in an SDXL positive prompt - the tokens "speed lines" are present and can pull lines into the baseline panel - and "clean background" fights the fixed subject sentence by stripping "soccer stadium, floodlights, crowd" toward a simple background. The baseline panel will not match the other panels' subject.
review.fix: Empty clause, like smear_style/none and aura/none already do. The baseline is the subject sentence alone; anything you type there is contamination.

review.issue: radial ("radial speed lines, emphasis lines radiating from the center") and impact ("impact lines, emphasis lines, burst lines") both resolve to the single danbooru feature "emphasis lines" radiating from centre. Same picture twice. The trailing "radiating from the center" is also prose rather than a tag.
review.fix: Keep radial as "speed lines, emphasis lines" and either drop impact or re-aim it at the thing that distinguishes it - the point of convergence on the subject: "impact frame, emphasis lines converging on the character, motion lines". If that still converges, drop it.

claim: Dropping the real background for an emotional field is standard anime grammar, not a shortcut - the world stops existing because the character has stopped noticing it. Void_black isolates and threatens, emotional_wash floods the frame with a single feeling, radial_burst detonates.

options.clause: detailed background, consistent with the scene
watercolor background, watercolor (medium), painted wash
photorealistic background, photographic backdrop
abstract background, flat color field
sunburst background, radial burst background, emphasis lines
patterned background, polka dot background, repeating motif
black background, void, empty darkness
white background, simple background, empty void
gradient background, monochrome color wash

review.issue: The "matched" clause "detailed background, consistent with the scene" is prose - "consistent with the scene" is an instruction to a human, not a tag - and "detailed background" is a quality push that makes the baseline panel busier than every other card's baseline.
review.fix: Empty clause, matching how anime.bg.hue_relation/matched and anime.color.harmony/free are already handled.

review.issue: Three options are already owned by other cards and will render the same: watercolor here vs anime.bg.style/watercolor, photobash here vs anime.bg.style/photobash, radial_burst here ("sunburst background, radial burst background, emphasis lines") vs shot.fx.screentone/flash_lines and shot.fx.speed_lines/radial.
review.fix: Decide the boundary: bg_treatment should own "replace the world with an emotional field" (void_black, white_void, abstract_color, emotional_wash, pattern) and hand the painting-medium options (watercolor, photobash) to anime.bg.style and the radiating-line options to speed_lines/screentone.

claim: Anime's symbolic emotion vocabulary is a genuine expressive channel, not decoration - a sweatdrop does work that no facial expression can do as fast. Reach for them when a beat needs to be legible in four frames, and be aware they instantly set a comic register.

options.clause: sweatdrop
anger vein, popped vein
blush lines, blush stickers
shock lines, emphasis lines on face, shaded face
sparkle, sparkles around head
teardrop, single tear
steam, steam from head
question mark, ?
chibi, super deformed, chibi inset

review.issue: chibi_pop ("chibi, super deformed, chibi inset") is not an emote symbol - it is anime.fx.deform_mode/sd_chibi plus mini_inset, and it will redraw the whole character while every other option in this card is a small addition, so the panel is not comparable to its neighbours. shock_lines ("shock lines, emphasis lines on face, shaded face") smuggles in "shaded face", which is the strongest tag in the clause and is exactly anime.fx.face_fault/shadowed_eyes - that panel will teach the face fault, not the shock lines.
review.fix: Delete chibi_pop; deform_mode owns it. shock_lines -> "shock lines, emphasis lines" with "shaded face" removed. Also add a "none" option with an empty clause - the card currently has no baseline to compare the symbols against.

claim: Manga screentone as a mood device is a different look entirely from film grain - it says the frame has stopped being a photograph and become a printed page. Flash_lines is a shock beat; mood_tone drops a flat tonal veil over a face that is thinking something bad.

options.clause: no screentone, flat color
screentone, halftone dots, benday dots
crosshatching, hatching, ink shading
gradient screentone, halftone gradient
flash lines, manga flash background, radiating ink lines
tonal overlay, monochrome shading, screentone wash

review.issue: The "none" clause "no screentone, flat color" is a negation plus a tag that belongs to a different variable - "flat color" is exactly anime.draw.shading_steps/flat_0's clause, so the screentone baseline arrives with the shading changed and is no longer comparable to the other five panels.
review.fix: Empty clause.

review.issue: mood_tone's clause is "tonal overlay, monochrome shading, screentone wash". "monochrome" is a very strong danbooru tag and will greyscale the entire frame, which is anime.color.setting/monochrome_memory, not a tonal veil. The only tag the model actually recognises in the clause is screentone, so what survives is either a greyscale image or a duplicate of the "dots" panel.
review.fix: Drop "monochrome" - try "screentone, halftone overlay, shaded face" if the intent is a veil over a thinking face, or cut the option, since dots/gradient/mood_tone are three names for one recognised feature.

claim: Sets how many video frames each drawing is held for, so a value of 3 gives the classic 8fps anime chug and 1 gives smooth full animation. A director drops to 1 only on the cut that has to feel fluid, because on-2s and on-3s is what makes footage read as drawn rather than filmed.
skip_reason: Drawing stepping only exists across frames. Every option produces the identical single frame, so a still panel cannot show any difference.

claim: Decides which parts of the frame get held on the step and which keep running smoothly, because real anime steps the drawings but pans the camera on every frame. Set it wrong and a beautiful pan judders like a broken projector.
skip_reason: This is a timing mask over a moving image; in one frame the stepped and unstepped elements are indistinguishable.

claim: One word that decides how much animation budget a cut is allowed to spend, from a frozen held drawing up to a showcase sequence that eats the episode's whole quota. A director spends showcase on maybe two cuts and pays for it by holding everything around them.
skip_reason: Allocates frame rate, motion strength and retries. All of that is temporal or pipeline; a single frame from a held cut and a showcase cut are the same drawing.

claim: Names how a shot stays alive while nothing is redrawn, whether that is a dead-still cel, a held drawing dragged across a painting, or a montage of stills. This is the backbone of limited animation and the cheapest screen time in the medium.
skip_reason: Every option describes what happens to one drawing over time. The still that starts a held_cel and the still that starts a held_pan are byte-identical.

claim: Picks the one or two elements that keep moving over an otherwise frozen drawing: a blink, a hair sway, a curl of steam. This is literally what limited animation is, and choosing the right element is what stops a held cut reading as a still image.
skip_reason: The variable selects which existing element animates, not whether it is present. Tagging 'steam' in a still adds steam to the frame instead of showing that the steam is the moving part.

claim: Declares that the motion is a seamless repeat rather than a one-off action, which lets a two-second generation cover eight seconds of screen time. Reach for it whenever a character is travelling, idling or a flag is flapping and nobody is watching the detail.
skip_reason: A cycle is defined by looping over time. A still of a running pose is char.movement, not proof that the motion repeats.

claim: Chooses the distortion drawing used to bridge two poses too far apart to tween: duplicated limbs, taffy stretch, or a single brushed streak. It is a drawn frame, not a post blur, and it is the difference between animation that punches and animation that slides.

options.clause: afterimage, multiple limbs, duplicated arms
stretched limbs, elongated arm, exaggerated distortion
smear frame, streaked motion blur, motion lines
afterimage, translucent trailing duplicate, motion trail
brushstroke smear, rough drawn blur, sketchy motion
dissolving arm, limb blurred away, motion blur

review.issue: multiples ("afterimage, multiple limbs, duplicated arms") and ghost_trail ("afterimage, translucent trailing duplicate, motion trail") both lead on "afterimage", which is the one danbooru tag doing all the work in each; they will produce the same drawing. streak ("smear frame, streaked motion blur, motion lines") and dissolve_limb ("dissolving arm, limb blurred away, motion blur") likewise both reduce to "motion blur".
review.fix: Give afterimage to ghost_trail only and rewrite multiples without it - "multiple arms, extra arms, duplicated limbs". For the blur pair, keep streak as "smear frame, motion lines" and drop dissolve_limb, or rewrite it as "blurry arm, motion blur, disappearing hand"; expect them to stay close.

claim: Says whether a repeated bank cut is the same footage played again, re-graded, or re-framed to disguise the repeat. It is a cost lever first and a look decision second, and audiences notice reuse_exact far faster than directors expect.
skip_reason: Reuse is a relationship between two shots. One panel cannot show whether the footage came from somewhere else.

claim: Declares which elements are cel-shaded 3D instead of drawn, from a single prop up to a fully CG shot. Modern anime mixes constantly, and stating the mix is the only way the 2D and 3D halves can be made to match instead of fighting. camera_3d is a motion option and renders as the baseline.

options.clause: cg prop, 3d model object, cel shaded
cg vehicle, 3d model car, cel shaded
cg crowd, 3d model background characters, cel shaded
cg environment, 3d model background, cel shaded
3dcg, cel shaded 3d, full cg render

review.issue: "none" and "camera_3d" both have empty clauses - two identical baseline panels in one card. Beyond that, SDXL cannot scope a render style to one named object: "cg prop, 3d model object, cel shaded", "cg vehicle...", "cg crowd...", "cg environment..." will each push the whole frame toward 3DCG, so the four scoped options plus full_3dcg largely converge. "cel shaded" also does no work here - it is what an anime checkpoint already draws.
review.fix: Mark camera_3d renderable:false per-option. For the rest, hang the 3d tag on the element and drop the dead "cel shaded" token - e.g. crowd_3d "3d, cg crowd, mmd background characters", environment_3d "3d background, cg scenery" - and expect props_3d/vehicles_3d to bleed globally. vehicles_3d additionally has no referent in the subject sentence (there is no vehicle in a soccer stadium), so it will either force an incongruous car onto the pitch or be ignored; consider dropping it.

claim: Bundles line, colour, finish and photographic artefacts into the decade an author actually thinks in, so 'ova_90s' delivers the whole package instead of eight separate sliders. It is the fastest way to date a film on purpose.

options.clause: retro artstyle, 1970s (style), cel animation, faded colors
retro artstyle, 1980s (style), cel animation, airbrush shading
retro artstyle, 1990s (style), ova screencap, cel animation
2000s (style), early digital anime, flat digital coloring
modern anime style, clean digital coloring, crisp lineart
modern anime screencap, glossy digital coloring, soft gradients
film grain, 35mm film look, faded colors, retro artstyle

review.issue: cel_70s ("retro artstyle, 1970s (style), cel animation, faded colors") and film_stock_retro ("film grain, 35mm film look, faded colors, retro artstyle") share "retro artstyle" + "faded colors" and will land in the same place - the model's grip on 1970s vs a faded film look is not that fine. film_stock_retro also duplicates anime.draw.cel_artifacts/film_grain, which is a different variable's job.
review.fix: Let era be decades only and delete film_stock_retro - photographic damage already lives in cel_artifacts. Keep the decade tags carrying the load ("1970s (style)", "1980s (style)") and drop the shared "retro artstyle, faded colors" tail from at least one of them so the panels can separate.

claim: The character-art equivalent of lens choice: hairline reads delicate and expensive, thick reads punchy and shounen, rough_genga reads like the key animation was shot before cleanup. It is the first thing the eye registers about a drawing.

options.clause: extremely thin lineart, hairline outlines
thin lineart, delicate outlines
clean lineart, even line weight
thick lineart, bold heavy outlines
tapered lineart, varying line weight, expressive lines
brush stroke lineart, inked brush lines
rough sketch, unfinished lineart, genga

review.issue: hairline ("extremely thin lineart, hairline outlines") and thin ("thin lineart, delicate outlines") will render identically - the model has one "thin lineart" feature and no degree control on it. Separately, rough_genga ("rough sketch, unfinished lineart, genga") is the same render as shot.fx.impact_frame/sketch_frame ("rough sketch, genga, pencil lines, unfinished drawing"); "rough sketch" dominates both.
review.fix: Drop hairline (or fold it into thin). For rough_genga, let line_weight own it and change impact_frame/sketch_frame to something that reads as a one-frame intrusion rather than a whole-drawing style - e.g. "rough sketch, monochrome, high contrast" - or accept the duplication and cut one.

claim: Whether the outline stays black or is traced in colour, which softens an entire film's character art without touching a single fill. Per-region trace is the expensive option houses use to make skin stop looking outlined in marker.

options.clause: black lineart, black outlines
dark grey lineart, softened outlines
colored lineart, colored outlines
colored inner lines, per region colored lineart
lineless, no outlines, painted edges

review.issue: "colored_trace_placeholder" is a leftover scaffold value, not a real option, and it carries an empty clause - so its panel is the untouched baseline, which is also what "black" ("black lineart, black outlines", already the model default) produces. Two of six panels are the same image and one of them is named placeholder.
review.fix: Delete colored_trace_placeholder from the enum. Give black an empty clause and treat it as the declared baseline, since black lineart is what the model does unprompted.

review.issue: color_trace ("colored lineart, colored outlines") and per_region_trace ("colored inner lines, per region colored lineart") will render the same way. "colored inner lines" is a real danbooru tag but it fires the same feature as "colored lineart"; "per region colored lineart" is invented phrasing the model cannot scope to skin vs hair vs cloth.
review.fix: Either drop per_region_trace, or differentiate it by naming the region the trace applies to in tag form - e.g. "colored inner lines, brown skin outlines, colored lineart on skin" - and accept it may still converge.

claim: How many hard shadow bands a drawing carries, which is the structural difference between anime and photography. flat_0 reads graphic and cheap, cel_2 is the industry default, painterly abandons cel logic entirely.

options.clause: flat color, no shading
cel shading, single shadow tone
cel shading, two tone shadows
cel shading, three tone shading, layered shadows
gradient shading, soft blended shadows
painterly shading, visible brushstrokes

review.issue: cel_1, cel_2 and cel_3 differ only by a shadow-band count ("single shadow tone" / "two tone shadows" / "three tone shading"). Animagine cannot count shadow bands; all three will land on ordinary two-tone cel shading. Three of six panels identical.
review.fix: Describe the visual consequence instead of the count, or collapse the middle: cel_1 -> "cel shading, single hard shadow, high contrast shading", cel_2 -> "cel shading" (declared default), cel_3 -> "layered shadows, detailed shading, dark rim shadow". If they still converge, drop cel_3.

claim: Cel shadows are hard by construction, so softening the edge is always a deliberate period or mood decision rather than a default. Hard reads modern and graphic; airbrush drags the whole frame back to 1985.

options.clause: hard shadow edges, crisp cel shadows
slightly softened shadow edges
soft shadows, blurred shadow edges
airbrush shading, smoothly blended shadows

review.issue: slightly_soft's clause is "slightly softened shadow edges" - prose, no tag, and a degree the model cannot hit. It will land on either the hard or the soft panel. soft ("soft shadows, blurred shadow edges") and airbrush ("airbrush shading, smoothly blended shadows") are also close enough to risk collapsing.
review.fix: Drop slightly_soft. Keep hard / soft / airbrush, and lean airbrush on its period identity where the model actually has signal: "airbrush, 1980s (style) shading".

claim: The colour a shadow shifts toward, chosen by a colour designer and worth roughly half a film's identity. Blue shift is the modern default and reads clean; warm shift reads nostalgic; grey multiply reads cheap and flat.

options.clause: shadows in a darker shade of the base color, monochromatic shading
blue shadows, cool toned shading
purple shadows, violet toned shading
complementary color shadows, contrasting hue shading
warm shadows, red toned shading
grey shadows, desaturated shading

review.issue: darker_same_hue's clause "shadows in a darker shade of the base color, monochromatic shading" is a sentence, not tags, and "monochromatic" risks pulling the whole frame toward greyscale - the opposite of what the option means. complementary ("complementary color shadows, contrasting hue shading") is not a tag either and against this subject (dark red hair, black jersey) will most likely just produce the same cool shadows as blue_shift.
review.fix: darker_same_hue -> empty clause and declare it the baseline (darker-same-hue is what the model does by default). complementary -> name the actual hue the subject implies, e.g. "green shadows, teal toned shading", or drop it.

claim: The shine band across the hair, which is one of the most reliable ways to date a film to a decade. angel_ring is 90s shoujo, segmented is the modern TV default, none reads as gritty or as a corpse.

options.clause: matte hair, no hair highlight
soft hair highlight, subtle sheen
angel ring hair highlight, halo shaped shine, shiny hair
segmented hair highlight, blocky hair shine
glossy hair, strong specular highlight
multiple hair highlight bands, layered hair shine

review.issue: The "none" clause "matte hair, no hair highlight" carries a negation that will be ignored while the words "hair highlight" stay in the conditioning. segmented ("segmented hair highlight, blocky hair shine") and multi_band ("multiple hair highlight bands, layered hair shine") are both "more than one band of shine" and will render the same.
review.fix: none -> "matte hair, dull hair" (positive only). Drop multi_band, or make it visibly different by count-free means: "shiny hair, two hair highlight bands, glossy" is not reliable, so cutting it is the safer call.

claim: House style for eye construction, set once above the whole cast because it is the single strongest signal of what kind of show this is. Big round eyes promise comedy and warmth; seinen_sharp promises somebody is going to get hurt.

options.clause: large round eyes, moe style eyes
very large eyes, shoujo style eyes, sparkling irises
bold angular eyes, thick eye outlines, shounen style
narrow sharp eyes, realistically proportioned eyes, seinen style
90s ova style eyes, small angular eyes, detailed iris
dot eyes, solid circle eyes, simplified eyes
realistic eyes, detailed iris, photorealistic eye

review.issue: minimal_dot ("dot eyes, solid circle eyes, simplified eyes") is the same clause as anime.fx.face_fault/dot_eyes ("dot eyes, solid circle eyes") - identical panels in two cards, and they mean different things (house style vs one-beat comedy face). realistic ("realistic eyes, detailed iris, photorealistic eye") is also risky: "photorealistic" on Animagine tends to drag the entire render off anime, so that panel will read as a style change rather than an eye change and will fight the subject.
review.fix: Let eye_render keep minimal_dot and delete dot_eyes from face_fault (face_fault still has swirl_eyes for the comedy register). Change realistic to "realistic eyes, detailed iris, semi-realistic" and drop "photorealistic".

claim: Line count per drawing, which is really a production tier: minimal is a weekly TV budget, film is a theatrical one. Push it up for hero shots and let it inherit low everywhere else, because ultra on every cut just reads as noise.

options.clause: minimal detail, simple shapes, few lines
tv anime detail, moderate detail
ova quality, high detail lineart
theatrical film quality, very detailed, intricate linework
extremely detailed, ultra detailed, intricate

review.issue: film ("theatrical film quality, very detailed, intricate linework") and ultra ("extremely detailed, ultra detailed, intricate") are both generic quality-boost token piles; on Animagine they hit the same aesthetic bucket and will render the same. "ova quality" and "theatrical film quality" are also not danbooru tags, so ova and film lean on "high detail"/"very detailed" and sit close too.
review.fix: Anchor the low end and let the high end be one option: minimal, tv_standard, and a single "detailed" tier ("extremely detailed, intricate details"). If five tiers must survive, differentiate by what gets the detail ("detailed background, detailed clothes" vs "detailed face, detailed eyes") rather than by intensity adverbs.

claim: The photographic damage that makes cel-era anime look old, added deliberately rather than inherited from a real camera. Halation and grain sell the age; the jitter and weave options sell it even harder but only once the clip moves.

options.clause: film grain, grainy texture
dust and scratches, damaged film, scratched print
halation, glowing highlight bloom, light bleed
paper texture, traditional media, textured overlay

review.issue: registration_jitter, telecine_wobble and gate_weave all carry empty clauses inside a renderable:true card, so they produce three byte-identical baseline panels sitting next to each other in the same card. The claim admits they only exist in motion, which is the right diagnosis but the wrong outcome.
review.fix: Give those three options an explicit per-option renderable:false (or move them into a separate motion-only variable marked renderable:false) so the card does not ship three duplicate stills. Keep film_grain, dust_scratches, halation and paper_texture, which do render. Also add a "none" baseline - as written every panel carries damage and there is nothing to compare against.

claim: The medium the background painting is made in, which is a separate axis from how finished it is and is what actually makes a film look painted rather than rendered. Watercolour reads gentle and hand-made; photobash reads modern, cheap and slightly uncanny against 2D characters.

options.clause: flat cel background, flat color scenery
poster color background, opaque flat painted scenery
watercolor (medium) background, watercolor wash scenery
gouache (medium) background, opaque matte painted scenery
acrylic paint (medium) background, matte painted scenery
airbrushed background, soft gradient scenery
digital painted background, detailed painted scenery
photorealistic painted background, hyperdetailed scenery
photobashed background, photographic texture scenery
line and wash background, ink lines with watercolor scenery
ukiyo-e background, woodblock print scenery
graphic flat background, minimalist vector scenery, flat color shapes

review.issue: poster_color ("opaque flat painted scenery"), gouache ("opaque matte painted scenery") and acrylic_matte ("matte painted scenery") differ only by a medium name the model has weak signal for plus the same two adjectives; they will render as one picture three times. digital_painted vs photoreal_painted vs photobash sit similarly close at the other end. Twelve options is also well past what this axis can actually resolve.
review.fix: Collapse to the mediums Animagine genuinely distinguishes: cel_flat, watercolor, gouache (keep one of the opaque-paint three), airbrush_soft, digital_painted, photobash, ukiyo_e, graphic_flat. Use the bare danbooru medium tag as the anchor - "gouache (medium)", "watercolor (medium)" - and drop the descriptive tails.

claim: Whether the background carries outlines at all, which quietly declares which anime tradition the film belongs to. Lineless painted backgrounds read filmic and expensive; full ink lines read graphic and manga-adjacent, and glue the background to the character art.

options.clause: lineless background, painted scenery without outlines
faint background lineart, soft outlined scenery
fully outlined background, background lineart
bold ink outlined background, heavy ink scenery

review.issue: The "none" clause "lineless background, painted scenery without outlines" ends in a prose negation. The positive tag "lineless" is doing all the work and is not the danbooru spelling.
review.fix: "no lineart, painted background" - drop the trailing clause.

claim: Pushes the background's hue away from the character's palette so the figure stays readable against a busy painting, which is a different tool from making it lighter or darker. Cooler is the safe separation; complementary is the loud one that makes a character look lit from another world.

options.clause: cooler toned background, blue shifted scenery
warmer toned background, orange shifted scenery
desaturated background, muted scenery colors
brighter background, high key scenery
darker background, low key scenery
complementary colored background, opposing hue scenery

review.issue: Every clause tries to scope a colour move to the background ("cooler toned background", "darker background, low key scenery"), but SDXL grades globally - the character will shift with the plate, which destroys the exact thing the variable exists to demonstrate (figure/ground separation). The results will also collide with anime.color.setting: lower_key reads as night, warmer reads as dusk, desaturated reads as storm.
review.fix: Keep the card but state the boundary in the clause with tags the model can localise - "blue background, cool background" rather than "cooler toned background, blue shifted scenery" - and cut lower_key and higher_key, which are indistinguishable from color.setting/night and color.setting/flashbulb once the grade goes global.

claim: How hard the character is welded into the painting behind them, which is generated anime's most common failure point. Without at least a contact shadow and matched line weight the figure reads as a sticker slapped onto a postcard.

options.clause: cutout character pasted on background, no contact shadow
background lineart matching character lineart, unified line weight
ambient color bleed onto character, background color reflected on subject
unified film grain over character and background
contact shadow under the character, ambient occlusion at the feet
fully composited character, matched grain lighting and lines, seamless integration

review.issue: Almost every clause is prose describing a compositing relationship, not danbooru tags: "background lineart matching character lineart, unified line weight", "ambient color bleed onto character, background color reflected on subject", "fully composited character, matched grain lighting and lines, seamless integration". None of those are tokens Animagine has any handle on, and the model has no way to express "the character is welded to the plate" as image content. line_match, color_bleed, shared_grain and full_comp will all return the ordinary baseline render, i.e. four identical panels, and "none" ("cutout character pasted on background, no contact shadow") will not produce a cutout either since the negation is ignored. This is the weakest card in the set.
review.fix: Cut it back to the one axis that has a real tag anchor and mark the rest non-renderable: keep none (empty clause, baseline) and ao_contact ("cast shadow, shadow under feet"), and either drop line_match / color_bleed / shared_grain / full_comp or set the whole variable renderable:false with a skip_reason saying integration is a compositing property of the render, not depictable content in a single still.

claim: How much wider than the delivered frame the background painting is made, which is the thing that makes a real anime pan possible instead of a digital crop. Panorama costs a lot of painting and buys a long, unbroken travelling shot.
skip_reason: The variable describes art outside the frame edges. Every option delivers the identical framed image; the difference only appears once the camera travels.

claim: States the palette rule so accent, rim and background colours can be derived instead of guessed shot by shot. Analogous holds a scene together; triad and duotone are the ones that make a frame look designed rather than merely coloured.

options.clause: analogous color scheme, neighbouring hues
complementary color scheme, two opposing hues
split complementary color scheme
triadic color scheme, three hue palette
monochromatic color scheme, single hue palette
duotone, two color palette
warm and cool split palette, warm key cool shadow

review.issue: complementary ("complementary color scheme, two opposing hues") and split_complementary ("split complementary color scheme") will render identically - the model has no representation of the split variant, and the clause is a colour-theory term rather than anything visual. triad is nearly as weak.
review.fix: Drop split_complementary. Keep the harmonies with real visual signatures (monochrome, duotone, warm_cool_split, complementary, analogous) and, if triad survives, name the hues: "triadic colors, red green blue palette".

claim: Anime approves a separate character colour set per lighting condition before any grade touches the frame, and this picks which set is in force. It is why a character under moonlight is repainted rather than just dimmed, and why memory scenes can go sepia without the grade fighting the art.

options.clause: night, dark blue color palette
evening, sunset colors, orange and purple light
dawn, sunrise light, pale pink glow
warm indoor lighting, tungsten glow
fluorescent lighting, green tinted white light
backlighting, strong rim light, dark front
moonlight, cool blue light
firelight, warm orange glow
underwater lighting, blue green caustics
storm light, desaturated grey, lightning glow
monochrome, greyscale
sepia, faded brown tones
camera flash, blown out white light, harsh flash

review.issue: underwater ("underwater lighting, blue green caustics") fights the fixed subject sentence - "underwater" is a strong scene tag and will flood the soccer stadium rather than relight it, so the panel stops being the same subject. backlit ("backlighting, strong rim light, dark front") is also the same render as anime.fx.silhouette_mode/rim_only.
review.fix: Drop underwater from this card - a lighting-condition card built on a stadium subject cannot demonstrate a submerged colour script. Keep backlit here and remove rim_only from silhouette_mode, so backlighting is taught once.

claim: The lettering style of the drawn sound word, which carries the whole tone of the moment: brushed katakana is a serious impact, latin comic lettering is a gag, hand scrawl is panic. Same sound, completely different scene.

options.clause: sound effects, katakana onomatopoeia, brush lettering
sound effects, kanji onomatopoeia, heavy calligraphy
sound effects, english onomatopoeia, comic book lettering
sound effects, handwritten scrawled onomatopoeia
sound effects, glitched digital lettering, chromatic aberration text

review.issue: katakana_brush and kanji_heavy both ask for CJK lettering, which Animagine renders as illegible glyph soup; brush katakana vs heavy calligraphic kanji will not be separable in the output. glitch also smuggles a global effect - "chromatic aberration text" will fringe the whole frame, not just the letters, so that panel changes the render rather than the lettering.
review.fix: Merge katakana_brush and kanji_heavy into one japanese-lettering option ("sound effects, japanese text, brush stroke lettering") and keep latin_comic and hand_scrawl, which differ by glyph shape rather than script. glitch -> "sound effects, glitched text" without the chromatic aberration.

claim: Where the sound word sits, which decides whether it reads as an impact landing on the subject or as a caption sitting politely in a corner. Every clause here has to carry a 'sound effects' anchor, because a position with nothing to position is not a picture.

options.clause: sound effects
sound effects, top left corner text
sound effects, top right corner text
sound effects, bottom left corner text
sound effects, bottom right corner text
sound effects, centered text
sound effects, text overlapping the character
sound effects, diagonal tilted lettering across the frame

review.issue: SDXL has no spatial conditioning from text, and "top left corner text" / "bottom right corner text" / "centered text" are not danbooru tags. tl, tr, bl, br and center will each drop garbled lettering wherever the sampler feels like it, so the five panels differ randomly rather than by option - the card teaches nothing and, worse, teaches something false if one panel happens to land in its corner.
review.fix: Keep only the options that are about relationship rather than coordinates - auto ("sound effects"), over_subject ("sound effects, text over the character") and diagonal ("sound effects, diagonal text") - and mark tl/tr/bl/br/center non-renderable, or set the whole variable renderable:false with skip_reason "quadrant placement is a layout parameter the sampler does not accept".

claim: Divides the frame so three reactions can land at once, which is something frame-in-frame cannot do. Diagonal shards are the shock version, manga panels are the stylised one, and inset PiP is how you keep a face on screen while showing what it is looking at.

options.clause: split screen, two vertical panels
split screen, two horizontal panels
split screen, three vertical panels
four panel grid, 2x2 panels
diagonal shard panels, shattered split screen
inset panel, small picture in picture corner panel
manga panels, comic page layout, panel gutters
radial wedge panels, pie sliced split screen

review.issue: two_v / two_h / three_v / grid_4 depend on the model counting panels, which it does not do reliably from phrases like "three vertical panels" - "split screen" is barely a tag. two_v and three_v in particular will be indistinguishable.
review.fix: Use the danbooru tags that actually encode panel layout: two_v/two_h -> "2koma", grid_4 -> "4koma", manga_panels -> "comic, panel layout", inset_pip -> "inset". Drop three_v, which has no tag and no reliable count.

claim: Swaps the character for a comedy design rather than applying an effect to them, which is why it belongs in its own variable. Chibi is the reset-the-stakes joke; noodle limbs and head pop are the ones that keep a character recognisable while breaking their anatomy.

options.clause: chibi, super deformed
oversized head, exaggerated head to body proportions
noodle limbs, boneless rubbery arms
rubber hose limbs, 1930s cartoon style
chibi inset panel, small super deformed figure in a corner box

claim: Says whether the comedy design takes the whole shot, sits in an inset box beside the real one, or hits for a single beat and leaves. A chibi cutaway and a chibi shot are different jokes with different timing. Each clause has to carry a chibi anchor because scope alone renders nothing, and punch_in_beat is pure timing.

options.clause: chibi, super deformed, full frame
chibi inset panel in the corner, main figure normally proportioned

review.issue: The card duplicates anime.fx.deform_mode. whole_shot ("chibi, super deformed, full frame") is the same render as deform_mode/sd_chibi ("chibi, super deformed"); inset ("chibi inset panel in the corner, main figure normally proportioned") is the same render as deform_mode/mini_inset ("chibi inset panel, small super deformed figure in a corner box"); punch_in_beat is empty, i.e. the plain baseline. Every panel in this card already exists in the other one. The inset clauses are also prose - the model will not honour "main figure normally proportioned" and will just chibify everything.
review.fix: Either mark the variable renderable:false with skip_reason "scope is a duration/layout decision; the two visible states are already covered by deform_mode", or delete the overlapping options from deform_mode and let deform_scope own whole_shot vs inset with tag-only clauses ("chibi, super deformed" vs "chibi inset, 2koma, inset panel").

claim: Redraws the face itself into a comedy or shock mask, which is a different channel from sticking a sweatdrop next to it. It is the loudest tonal switch in the anime toolkit: one shadowed-eyes frame turns a friendly scene sinister.

options.clause: jaw drop, wide open mouth, shocked expression
@_@, swirl eyes, dizzy
dot eyes, solid circle eyes
shaded face, shadowed eyes
nosebleed, comedic nosebleed
half shaded face, shocked expression, comedic horror face
streaming tears, comedic tear fountain, crying
soul leaving body, small ghost floating above, comedic

claim: Effects animation is its own craft and looks nothing like photographic fire or water, so this names the drawn element directly. Cel fire and crystal water are the ones that instantly say 'this was animated by hand'; geometric debris is the modern action-show signature.

ink smoke, brushy black smoke plume

stylized lightning, jagged electric bolts
