claim: A drawn element attached to the character and held across the whole shot, which is how anime states power, menace or infatuation without a line of dialogue. Dark miasma and pressure ripple are threat; sparkle is the joke version of the same grammar.

options.clause: glowing aura, soft light aura
flaming aura, fire aura
electric aura, crackling lightning aura
dark aura, black miasma, ominous smoke
sparkle aura, sparkles
pressure ripple aura, shockwave rings, air distortion

review.issue: sparkle ("sparkle aura, sparkles") is the same render as shot.fx.emote_symbols/sparkles ("sparkle, sparkles around head") - the "sparkle" tag dominates both and puts sparkles around the character either way.
review.fix: Keep sparkles as the emote symbol (short comic beat) and either drop aura/sparkle or make it a held field rather than a garnish: "sparkle background, glowing aura, sparkles".

claim: Reduces the character to a flat shape, which is stock anime grammar for a reveal, a threat, or a moment where identity is being withheld. Rim-only is the cheat that keeps them readable; full silhouette throws away the design entirely and dares the audience to recognise the outline. strobe_silhouette is a timing pattern and renders as the baseline.

options.clause: silhouette, solid black figure, featureless
colored silhouette, flat single color figure
backlighting, dark figure with bright rim outline

review.issue: "none" and "strobe_silhouette" both have empty clauses, so those two panels are the identical baseline image. Separately, rim_only ("backlighting, dark figure with bright rim outline") is the same render as anime.color.setting/backlit ("backlighting, strong rim light, dark front"), and full_silhouette ("silhouette, solid black figure, featureless") is the same render as shot.fx.impact_frame/silhouette_pop.
review.fix: Mark strobe_silhouette renderable:false per-option so it is not shown as a panel. Then decide which card owns backlighting and which owns silhouette - drop rim_only here (it is a lighting state) and drop silhouette_pop from impact_frame (or restrict it to "silhouette, high contrast, one frame flash"), so the two cards stop teaching the same picture.

claim: How many distinct mouth positions the lip sync draws from, which is the structural difference between anime and a Western cartoon: three positions reads Japanese, full viseme reads dubbed. Raise it only when a face is close and talking for a long time.
skip_reason: A chart is a set of positions used over time. A still can only show one mouth, which says nothing about how many exist.

claim: Whether the mouths were animated to the recording or the recording came after, which is why loose sync is correct in Japanese anime rather than a defect. Tight prescored sync on an anime face reads immediately as a dub.
skip_reason: Defined by the relationship between an audio track and a moving mouth. There is no audio in a still and no motion to be in or out of sync.

claim: The shape of a blink, which is a performance beat rather than an idle tic: a double blink is surprise, a slow close is resignation, held shut is refusal to look. Rate alone cannot tell those apart, which is why the pattern gets its own word.
skip_reason: Every option except held_shut is defined by timing between frames, and held_shut alone is just closed eyes, which char.mouth-style expression tags already cover. Panels would be identical or misleading.

claim: Marks which piece of broadcast furniture a chapter is, which drives entirely different music, caption and pacing rules than its dramatic role does. An avant and a C-part can carry the same scene and still need opposite treatment.
skip_reason: Structural position inside an episode. Nothing about where a shot sits in the running order is visible in the shot itself.

claim: The form the opening takes, which is a short film with its own grammar rather than a scene: a character-intro OP sells the cast, an action showcase sells the budget, a typography OP sells the mood. Pick it before writing a single shot of the OP.
skip_reason: Every option describes how dozens of shots are assembled over ninety seconds. One frame pulled from a montage OP and a dance OP with the same subject is the same frame.

claim: The form of the ending, usually the cheapest and most stylised part of an anime: an illustration gallery costs almost nothing, a single-take walk costs one very good shot, an epilogue scene costs a whole scene. It sets what the audience is left holding.
skip_reason: A sequence shape defined across a full credit roll. The difference between a still pan ED and a single-take walk ED cannot exist inside one frame.

claim: How many act-break cards the episode carries, which is structural punctuation the audience feels even when they cannot name it. A paired eyecatch splits the episode cleanly in half; none makes a 22-minute episode feel like one long breath.
skip_reason: This is a count of structural cards in an episode, not a look. anime.format.eyecatch_style is where the visible design lives.

claim: The design of the act-break card itself, a tiny authored image that tells the audience what kind of show this is. A logo card says prestige, a chibi gag says the stakes reset every week, a silhouette card says somebody is still hiding something.

options.clause: logo card, centered emblem, flat graphic background
pin-up pose card, single posed figure, plain flat background
still life insert, single object close-up, plain background
chibi, super deformed comedic pose, flat background
large decorative title typography, text card
silhouette, solid figure on flat color background

review.issue: prop_still ("still life insert, single object close-up, plain background") is unrenderable under this method — the subject sentence mandates "1boy, solo, male focus" plus full character description, so the panel will be the boy, not a prop. It will not show what the option does. Also, five of the six clauses carry a flat/plain background tag against the subject's "soccer stadium, floodlights, crowd", so most of the card ends up measuring whether the background override wins rather than the differences between card designs.
review.fix: Mark prop_still renderable:false at the option level (or accept it is a known-invalid panel and say so). For the rest, standardise the background tag to one identical phrase across all options — e.g. always "simple background" — so the only thing varying between panels is the card design itself ("logo", "chibi", "silhouette", "text") rather than five different phrasings of "flat".

claim: The shape of the next-episode tease, a fixed anime form with its own voice and pacing: clips with voice-over is the standard, tease-only withholds everything, gag previews break the fourth wall. It is the last thing the audience hears and sets what they come back for.
skip_reason: Built from voice-over plus a cut of clips. Both the audio and the multi-shot assembly are outside what a single frame can carry.

claim: Declares what kind of container the shot sits inside, which settles in one word where light comes from, whether weather is visible at all, and how sound behaves. A director sets this before anything else because interior, underwater and void are three different physics, not three set dressings.

outdoors, open sky, natural light

underground, tunnel, concrete walls, dim lighting

midair, high altitude, clouds below, aerial view

review.issue: The aerial clause smuggles a camera control: "aerial view" is a danbooru framing tag meaning the camera looks down from above, so this panel changes the shot angle as well as the container. It will read as evidence about a shot-angle variable, not about interior_exterior.
review.fix: "midair, high altitude, clouds below, falling" — keep the figure's position in the world, drop the camera instruction.

review.fix: "plain stone architecture, unadorned walls, blank facades" — three positives, no negation.

claim: How advanced the working machinery is, kept deliberately separate from period so a feudal world can carry magitech and a far-future one can be pre-industrial. It decides whether a character reaches for a torch, a switch or a hologram.

review.fix: Positive only: "torch, oil lamp, hand tools, wooden cart". Push "machinery, wires, electric light" into the negative prompt if the floodlights bleed through.

claim: One word that moves foliage, wardrobe, sun angle and ambience at the same time. Directors set it because the same scene played in late_summer and in winter are two different stories about the same people.

review.issue: The card leans on foliage, but the fixed subject is a floodlit stadium with essentially no plant life beyond pitch grass. spring, autumn and winter will survive on petals/leaves/snow; early_summer ("fresh green leaves, verdant foliage"), late_summer ("dry grass, cicada shell, hazy heat") and dry_season ("cracked earth, brown grass, dust") have nothing to attach to and are likely to collapse into each other and into summer.
review.fix: For the three foliage-dependent options, add one cue that survives a stadium without stealing another variable — e.g. late_summer -> "heat haze, dry brown grass, harsh white light"; dry_season -> "dust in the air, cracked bare ground"; early_summer -> "bright fresh green turf, clear light". If they still cannot separate, say so on the card rather than shipping three identical panels.

review.issue: The fixed subject sentence ends in "crowd", which is the exact axis this card tests. Every panel therefore ships a hard-coded crowd token that the option clause has to fight, and "empty"/"sparse" fight it with a negation ("no spectators") — CLIP has no negation, so that phrase reliably summons spectators. empty, sparse and moderate are likely to land in the same place.
review.fix: Drop all negations and go positive: empty -> "empty stands, vacant seats, deserted bleachers"; sparse -> "scattered spectators, half-empty stands, gaps in the seating". This is also the one card where the subject sentence itself needs an exception — render this set with "crowd" removed from the subject, otherwise the card is measuring token tug-of-war, not the variable.

skip_reason: Every value in this enum names a sound, not a visible thing. Cicadas, crickets, frogs, wind chimes, distant traffic, school noise, machinery, waves and river all select an ambience stem at mix time; none of them changes a pixel of a still. A clause that drew a visible cicada or visible waves would be silently testing set dressing (world.biome, world.air_particles) under this variable's name, and the resulting panels would be evidence about the wrong control.

claim: Type declares what object you are actually making — a 90-second short, a 24-minute episode and a 3-minute music video want different scene lengths, different density and different obligations about whether an ending is required. It is the first question asked because every downstream default inherits from it.
skip_reason: Duration and structural obligation, not appearance. The same frame of the same boy is pixel-identical whether it belongs to a loop, a trailer or a feature, so all eight panels would collapse into one image.

claim: Structure hands each chapter a default dramatic role so pacing and music arcs can be derived instead of hand-authored per chapter. Kishotenketsu buys you a turn without needing a conflict; three_act buys you a conflict and then demands you resolve it.
skip_reason: Describes how chapters are arranged across the whole runtime. It is a claim about ordering between scenes, and a single still contains no ordering — nothing in the frame changes when the skeleton does.

claim: One word tells pacing, music and grade what this chapter is for, so a cold_open can run hot and an epilogue can run cool without per-shot notes. Normally derived from position, but you override it when you want an act break to behave like an interlude.
skip_reason: A positional label inside the structure. 'ten' and 'act2' are assertions about where we are in the film, not about how anything looks; the visual consequences arrive through the pacing and grade defaults it seeds, not through the frame itself.

review.issue: Four of six clauses are prose abstractions with no danbooru equivalent — "detached observation", "uninvolved", "character-aligned vantage", "close emotional proximity", "all-seeing", "two viewpoints" render nothing. objective and subjective will differ only by "shallow focus", and objective vs omniscient only by "elevated". skip_reason: Relational, not visual: earlier and later are only meaningful against another shot. In isolation a still cannot say which side of the spine it sits on, and the treatment that would sell it (haze, desaturation) actually belongs to story.reality_layer — rendering it here would just duplicate that card.

claim: Declaring a narrator reserves mix headroom for voice-over before a single line is written, and tells the edit that shots must breathe under speech instead of cutting on the action. A diary and an omniscient VO are different contracts with the audience about who is telling this and how much they know.
skip_reason: none, char_vo and omniscient_vo are pure audio and change nothing in a frame. The text-bearing options (text_card, diary, letter) are composited insert graphics inserted between shots, not a treatment of the subject panel — and Animagine cannot render legible text, so those panels would show typographic noise rather than the option.

claim: Cards are structural furniture — main title, chapter, location, time, end — and should never cost you a hand-built shot. Declaring one lets the edit drop it at the boundary with the right hold length and the right music sting attached.
skip_reason: Every option is a text graphic composited in ffmpeg over or between shots, so the subject panel is identical for all six. SDXL also renders legible text unreliably, meaning a render would document the model's spelling failures rather than the variable.

claim: Content flags are a declaration, not a look: they drive audience warnings, auto-populate the negative prompt and soften flash and strobe fx automatically. You set them because the scene already contains the thing — the flag never puts it there.
skip_reason: Setting a flag gates and warns rather than generating; it subtracts from the prompt more often than it adds. flashing_lights is temporal by definition, sexual_content is something we will not render at all, and blood or injury appear in a frame only because the shot's own content put them there — which is a different variable's job.

claim: Declares what the character is for in the story so the pipeline can spend on them — prompt priority, face-weight budget, how often they anchor a shot. A director sets it once per character to stop an extra eating the token budget that belongs to the lead.
skip_reason: Role is a budget and priority setting, not a look. With the subject sentence and seed held fixed, a lead and an extra are the same drawing; the only way to make the panels differ is to smuggle in shot size, framing or wardrobe, which belong to other variables. Nothing here changes pixels on its own.

review.fix: Hold one primary fixed and enumerate real secondary values against it, one panel each. e.g. primary is always "smile" in the subject-adjacent slot, then options: none ("smile"), grief ("smile, teary eyes"), anger ("smile, furrowed brow, tense jaw"), fear ("smile, wide eyes, sweatdrop"), exhaustion ("smile, half-closed eyes, eye bags"), contempt ("smile, half-lidded eyes, one raised eyebrow"). Both also collide with light.quality.overcast_flat, light.ratio.flat_1_1 and light.key_dir.ambient_none, so four cards would ship the same image.
review.fix: Give sky_ambient the thing that actually distinguishes open shade — colour and sky direction: "overcast sky, cool blue-grey daylight, soft shadowless light from above". Make unmotivated the empty-clause baseline panel, since that is literally what it is: the generator default nobody chose. Then delete ambient_none from light.key_dir (see separate note) and let light.quality own overcast_flat.

claim: Where the main light sits on the compass around the subject, which is the single biggest control over how a face is shaped. Front flattens and reassures, side splits the face into a lit half and a hidden half, and back throws the whole read away and keeps only the outline.

options.clause: frontal lighting, lit straight on, flat face with no side shadow
lit from the front left, light on the left of the face, soft shadow on the right
lit from the front right, light on the right of the face, soft shadow on the left
side lighting from the left, half lit face, hard shadow over the right half
side lighting from the right, half lit face, hard shadow over the left half
backlit from rear left, rim light along the left edge, face in shadow
backlit from rear right, rim light along the right edge, face in shadow
backlighting, contre-jour, glowing outline, face in shadow
top-down lighting, light from directly above, shadowed eye sockets
underlighting, lit from below, upward cast shadows on the face
ambient light only, no key light, flat shadowless illumination

review.issue: top ("top-down lighting, light from directly above, shadowed eye sockets") and bottom ("underlighting, lit from below, upward cast shadows on the face") are elevation, not azimuth, and duplicate light.key_elev.overhead ("light from directly overhead, top-down lighting, black eye sockets") and light.key_elev.below ("underlighting, light from below, upward cast shadows, lit chin") almost word for word. The card's own claim says key_dir is "where the main light sits on the compass" — top and bottom are not on the compass. ambient_none is not a direction either.
review.fix: Cut top, bottom and ambient_none from light.key_dir and let light.key_elev own the vertical axis and light.motivation.unmotivated own the sourceless case. That leaves key_dir a clean 8-point azimuth, which is also the only way the two cards read as different variables when an author flips between them.

claim: How high the key sits vertically, separate from which side it comes from. Below is the campfire horror angle, above is normal and flattering, and overhead hollows the eyes out and makes a character look condemned.

options.clause: underlighting, light from below, upward cast shadows, lit chin
light at eye level, horizontal key, almost no nose shadow
light from above, downward shadows under the brow and nose
steep light from high above, deep eye socket shadows, short nose shadow
light from directly overhead, top-down lighting, black eye sockets, bright lit hair

claim: The hardness of the shadow edge, which is the emotional temperature of a location before any colour is applied. Hard light is cruel and specific, very soft is tender and forgiving, and specular_wet is the only one that changes the skin itself rather than the shadows.

options.clause: hard light, sharp shadow edges, high contrast shadows
medium light, moderately defined shadow edges
soft lighting, soft shadow edges, gentle falloff
very soft diffused light, edgeless shadows, wrapping light
overcast flat lighting, shadowless, dull even illumination
specular highlights, wet glossy skin, sharp bright speculars

claim: How dark the shadow side is allowed to get relative to the key, which is the numeric handle on drama. Flat_1_1 is comedy and daytime television, chiaroscuro_16_1 is a confession scene, and silhouette throws the face away entirely to buy a shape.

options.clause: flat lighting, evenly lit face, no shadow side
gentle key to fill contrast, slightly darker shadow side
classic lighting ratio, clearly darker shadow side, shadow detail retained
dramatic lighting, deep black shadow side, narrow bright key side
chiaroscuro, sliver of light on the face, surrounded by blackness
silhouette, black featureless figure, backlit shape

review.issue: The clauses are camera-department jargon rather than tags: "gentle key to fill contrast, slightly darker shadow side" and "classic lighting ratio, clearly darker shadow side, shadow detail retained". Danbooru has no vocabulary for key-to-fill ratios, so low_2_1 and normal_4_1 will land on the model as noise plus the weak phrase "darker shadow side" and will very likely render as the same mildly shaded face. Only flat_1_1, chiaroscuro_16_1 and silhouette have real tag equivalents.
review.fix: Rewrite in what the shadow looks like, which the tag space does have: low_2_1 "soft shadow on one cheek, open shadows, low contrast"; normal_4_1 "clear shadow on one side of the face, visible shading, moderate contrast"; dramatic_8_1 "high contrast, deep black shadow side, narrow lit strip". Drop the numeric ratio language from the clause entirely — it belongs in the value name, not in the prompt.

claim: What happens inside the shadow, which is the difference between moody and muddy. Bounce and soft_fill keep information alive in the dark side, negative_fill actively subtracts light to sculpt a jaw, and none lets the shadow go to pure black.

options.clause: no fill light, unlit black shadow side
bounced fill light, faint light returning into the shadow side
soft fill light, open shadows, low contrast shading
negative fill, deepened shadow side, darkened cheek edge
cool blue ambient sky fill, blue light in the shadows

review.issue: Same jargon problem, worse: "bounced fill light, faint light returning into the shadow side", "negative fill, deepened shadow side, darkened cheek edge", "soft fill light, open shadows, low contrast shading". "Fill", "bounce" and "negative fill" are crew words with no danbooru presence, and the residual instructions (bounce = a bit of light in the shadow, soft_fill = open shadows) are also what light.ratio.low_2_1 asks for. bounce, soft_fill and negative_fill are the three most likely to come back indistinguishable; only ambient_sky has a hook the model understands, and that hook is its colour.
review.fix: Describe the contents of the shadow, not the instrument: none "pitch black shadows, crushed shadow side"; bounce "faint detail visible in the shadows, dark but readable shadow side"; soft_fill "open shadows, evenly lit, low contrast shading"; negative_fill "darkened cheek edge, shadow deepening toward the jaw"; ambient_sky "blue shadows, cool blue light in the shadow side". If bounce and soft_fill still will not separate, the honest move is to merge them rather than ship two identical panels.

claim: The edge highlight that peels a character off the background, and the most identifiably anime lighting device there is. Subtle just separates, halo turns the character into an event, and none is a deliberate choice to let them sink into the world.

options.clause: no rim light, edges blending into the background
subtle rim light, faint edge highlight
strong rim light, bright hard outline on hair and shoulders
halo backlight, glowing full outline, hair haloed with light
a single small rim highlight, light just kissing one shoulder edge
double rim light, bright edges on both sides, two opposing kickers

review.issue: kiss is written as prose — "a single small rim highlight, light just kissing one shoulder edge" opens with an article and a relative clause, which is exactly the phrasing that turns Animagine to mush. It also asks for the same thing as subtle ("subtle rim light, faint edge highlight") plus a shoulder restriction the model has no reliable handle for.
review.fix: Tag it: "faint rim light on one shoulder, asymmetric edge highlight". Be ready to merge kiss into subtle if the renders match — a one-shoulder restriction is a very thin axis to spend a panel on.

claim: The light sources actually visible in the frame, declared once so every shot agrees where the glow is coming from. Practicals are how a night scene gets a reason to exist, and swapping a candle for a monitor changes the century of the scene without touching anything else.

options.clause: neon sign, glowing neon tubing, coloured sign glow
desk lamp, warm lamp glow, small pool of light
ceiling fluorescent tubes, cold overhead strip lighting
candle, candlelight, small warm flame
fireplace, burning fire, orange firelight
computer monitor, glowing screen, blue screen glow
phone screen, glowing cellphone, face lit from below by a phone
streetlight, glowing street lamp, cone of light
lantern, glowing paper lantern, warm hanging light
car headlights, glaring headlight beams
moonlight through a window, pale window light, moonlit interior
stage lights, spotlight beam, lighting rig
vending machine, glowing vending machine, bright box of light

review.issue: The clauses fight the fixed subject sentence, which already contains "soccer stadium, floodlights, crowd" — i.e. an exterior that already names its own practical. candle, fireplace, desk_lamp, monitor, phone_screen, moon_window, vending_machine and ceiling_fluoro all require an interior or a street, so those panels will document the tag losing a fight with the stadium rather than showing the practical. At the other end, stage_light and streetlight are so close to floodlights that they may read as no-ops. There is also no "none" baseline in this enum, unlike every comparable card.
review.fix: Run this card (and the window-dependent options of light.shadow_gobo: blinds, curtain, window_cross) on a second fixed subject sentence with a neutral interior — same boy, same seed, "indoors, dark room, night" instead of the stadium — and say so in the card. Also add a "none" value with an empty clause so the baseline is on the sheet.

claim: The pattern cut into the light before it lands, which is the highest value per token lighting device available in tag space. Blinds across a face say interrogation, dappled foliage says summer afternoon, and none of it costs you a new location.

options.clause: unbroken clean shadows, no patterned shadow
window blind shadows, venetian blind stripes across the face
dappled shadows, leaf shadows, dappled light
branch shadows, bare tree branch pattern cast across the frame
grate shadow, metal grid shadow pattern
curtain shadow, soft draped fabric shadow
shadows of a crowd, overlapping human silhouette shadows
rain streak shadows, running water shadow pattern on skin
water caustics, rippling light patterns
window frame shadow, cross-shaped pane shadow

claim: The colour relationship between the key and everything filling in behind it, which buys depth without adding a single light. Teal_orange is the blockbuster reflex, cool_key_warm_rim is the anime night reflex, and monochrome_wash flattens the frame into one emotional colour on purpose.

options.clause: neutral white lighting, no colour contrast between sources
warm key light, cool blue shadows
cool blue key light, warm orange rim light
teal and orange lighting, orange highlights, teal shadows
magenta and cyan lighting, pink key light, cyan fill
sodium vapour lighting, amber monochrome night, orange cast
single colour light wash, monochromatic lighting
warm candlelight on one side, cold moonlight on the other

claim: How the light behaves over time rather than what it looks like, and the thing that stops an i2v clip reading as a moving photograph. A director reaches for it when the scene needs a pulse the camera and the actor are not providing.
skip_reason: Every option here is a modulation over time, and a still shows exactly one instant of it. flicker, pulse, breathing_glow and candle all resolve to the same lit frame; strobe and lightning would render as an arbitrary bright or dark moment that says nothing about the behaviour; passing_lights and tv_wash depend on the sweep, not the state. Any clause written here would be indistinguishable from light.motivation and would sell a claim the still cannot support. This card belongs in the LTX motion test set, one clip per option, not the still set.

claim: Whether the air itself is visible as shafts of light, which turns empty space into a graphic element. Subtle adds atmosphere, strong makes the light a character in the frame, and dusty is the one that also tells you the room has been shut up for years.

options.clause: clear air, no light shafts
faint light rays, soft light shafts
god rays, bold volumetric light beams, sunbeam
dusty light shafts, dust motes in the beams, hazy air
underwater light rays, rippling caustic shafts through water

claim: The catchlight, which is the smallest mark on the frame and the one that decides whether a character is alive. Killing it reads instantly as death, possession or menace, and anime_sparkle pushes the other way into open adoration.

options.clause: no catchlight, matte unreflective eyes
small catchlight, single highlight in each eye
bright large catchlights, glossy reflective eyes
sparkling eyes, glittering highlights in the eyes
dead eyes, empty eyes, no highlights in the eyes

review.issue: none ("no catchlight, matte unreflective eyes") and dead_flat ("dead eyes, empty eyes, no highlights in the eyes") are the same instruction written twice — remove the highlight from the eyes. Two of the five panels are asking for one thing.
review.fix: Make none an empty clause (the baseline catchlight Animagine gives you unasked, which is the useful comparison), and let dead_flat keep the removal using the real tags: "empty eyes, dead eyes, no light in the eyes" with "catchlight" pushed to the negative prompt.

claim: The hard band of shadow dropped across the eyes, anime's standing notation for menace, dissociation or a character who has stopped being safe. Full hides them completely, glint_only leaves one point of light inside the dark and is the villain reveal.

options.clause: clearly visible eyes, no shadow across the eyes
shadow across the upper half of the eyes, shaded brow, pupils still visible
shaded face, eyes obscured by shadow, dark band across the eyes
shaded face, eyes hidden in shadow, single bright glint, glowing eyes

claim: Buys resolution after the diffusion pass, so a hero shot can carry the line detail that survives a big screen while a two-second cutaway stays cheap. Reach for it only on shots held long enough for the audience to inspect them; upscaling everything multiplies render time for detail nobody sees at cut speed.
skip_reason: Post-generation resolution pass, not a prompt input. With the subject sentence and seed fixed the prompt is byte-identical across all four values, so every panel is the same image at a different pixel count. Tags like 'absurdres' or 'highres' would fake it by asking the model for a different, busier drawing, which is not what an upscaler does. Compare it instead by rendering one seed and running the upscaler at each factor, inspected at 100% - a resolution test, not a capability card.

claim: Bridges the gap between the frame rate the video model actually generated and the delivery fps. to_movie_fps is the honest fill; double and smooth invent motion that sands the deliberate on-2s and on-3s stepping off your animation, turning limited animation into soap-opera glide.
skip_reason: Purely temporal - it exists only in the gaps between frames. A still cannot show the difference between native and interpolated motion, and the specific thing that matters here (whether interpolation smears the anime stepping into mush) is invisible in any single image. Needs a side-by-side clip at matched playback speed, ideally on a fast pan where the judder is most legible.

claim: Declares what the numbers in the file actually mean, so a grade built in preview still looks like itself after encode. rec709 is the correct default for video delivery, srgb for web stills, rec2020 only when the entire downstream chain honours it - otherwise the wide primaries get clipped back and every saturation decision lands wrong.
skip_reason: An encode-time transfer and primaries declaration, not something the prompt can express. Animagine emits the same pixels regardless of this setting; in a correctly managed chain all three values look identical, and when they visibly differ that is a mismatch bug rather than a look. Simulating it with saturation or contrast tags would document a grade, not a colour space, and would teach the author the wrong lesson.

claim: Decides who can open the file and how much of the grade survives the squeeze. h264 when it simply has to play everywhere, prores when the cut goes back into an edit or a second grade pass, h265/vp9/av1 when file size beats compatibility. Flat cel colour and hard line art are exactly what cheap codecs band and ring.
skip_reason: Codecs apply to video encoding; a still is never encoded as h264 or prores. The real content of the variable - banding across flat cel fills, mosquito noise crawling on hard line art, how much grade headroom is left - only appears after compression at a real bitrate over real motion. Needs an encoded-clip comparison viewed at 100%, on a shot with large flat colour areas and a gradient sky.

claim: Governs how much of the last render you pay for a second time. reuse_unless_changed is the working default; force when you suspect a stale cache is lying to you; never for a clean final; reuse when you have only touched the edit and want every shot left exactly as it was.
skip_reason: Has no visual signature by design - a correct cache produces output identical to a fresh render, and that identity is the whole point of the feature. The only things that change are wall-clock time and whether a stale asset slips through. All four panels would be the same image, so there is nothing for a card to show.

claim: Decides which shots exist first while a long render is still grinding. hero_first puts the shots that decide the film in front of you in minutes instead of an hour; cheap_first gets you a complete rough cut fastest; dependency respects what feeds what; sequential is for when you want to watch the film assemble in order.
skip_reason: Pure scheduling. It changes when each shot lands on disk and never what any shot looks like. Every panel would be the identical frame. If an author wants to see this variable at work the artefact is a render-queue timeline, not an image.

claim: Says whether a broken shot stops the film or quietly becomes part of it. retry absorbs transient VRAM and network flakes; halt is for a final where a silent hole is unacceptable; warn_continue and placeholder are for overnight drafts, where waking to a watchable cut with gaps beats waking to a render that died at shot four.
skip_reason: A failure-handling policy that only manifests when generation actually fails. On a successful render all four values produce the same frame; the difference lives in the log and in whether the finished film has a hole in it. It cannot be provoked by a prompt clause, and staging a fake failure would be demonstrating the placeholder variable instead of this one.

claim: Decides whether a rough cut containing a failed shot is still watchable. keyframe_still holds the shot's own frame so timing and continuity survive the gap; last_good hides the failure but lies about what the cut does; slate labels the hole so nobody grades a broken shot by accident; black is honest and brutal.
skip_reason: The four values are substituted frames, not prompted content: a black fill, a text slate, a frame borrowed from a different shot, and the shot's own keyframe. None can be produced by adding a tag clause to a fixed subject sentence - black and slate would have to erase the subject entirely, which breaks the method's core rule, and Animagine cannot render legible slate text. The right demo is compositing all four substitutions into a real cut and watching it, which is a pipeline demo rather than a tag comparison.

claim: Marks a cut as provisional so a work-in-progress is never mistaken for the finished film once it leaves your hands. draft for internal circulation, version_slate when notes need to cite a specific build, custom for client or festival marking, none only when you genuinely mean final.
skip_reason: The mark is burned on by ffmpeg after generation and never by the diffusion model. Prompting 'watermark', 'artist name' or 'english text' would only demonstrate SDXL's garbled-lettering failure mode, which is the precise opposite of the clean legible overlay the option delivers - the card would teach the author to distrust a feature that works fine. Show it instead as an ffmpeg overlay applied over one identical render, four times.

claim: The film's frame clock — every shot duration, ease curve and fx interval is quantised against it. 24 is the film default; 8 and 12 force a visibly stepped, hand-drawn cadence, while 60 buys a smoothness that reads as camcorder and fights the anime look.
skip_reason: Frame rate is pure timing. A single still has no frame clock, so all seven panels would come back byte-identical — the difference only exists once two frames sit next to each other in time.

claim: Delivery pixel size, separate from aspect and from the oversized frame you actually render into. Drop to 832x480 while you are iterating and want turnaround; save 1920x1080 for shots that will be looked at closely, because it costs real time on every retry.
skip_reason: A render/delivery setting, not content. Nothing in the prompt moves it — pixel size comes from the SDXL latent dimensions, so panels would differ only in how much detail the sampler had room for, and any clause claiming to express it would be a lie. If an author needs to see it, render the same prompt at each size; that is a resolution test, not a capability card.

claim: The shape of the frame, which every composition default is derived from — where the horizon can sit, how much lookroom exists, whether a standing figure fills the frame or floats in it. 2.39:1 strands a lone figure in negative space; 9:16 crops the world away until the character is the entire image.
skip_reason: Genuinely visible in a still, but not reachable from tags. Frame shape comes from the latent dimensions, and Animagine will not reshape the canvas because the prompt says '2.39:1' — the nearest tag, letterboxed, belongs to shot.frame.letterbox and only fakes the two widest values. Showing this honestly needs one render per ratio at its native resolution, which changes the latent and therefore breaks the identical-seed rule this method depends on.

claim: Decides whether every resolved variable emits danbooru tags or English prose, rewriting the output of every prompt builder in the film. danbooru is the only mode SDXL parses reliably — natural exists for models and captioners that want sentences, and choosing it turns a working prompt into mush.
skip_reason: This variable rewrites the subject sentence itself — the one thing the method holds fixed — so there is no clause position for it to occupy. Its three values are prompt formats, not image content, and the only observable difference (prose returning abstract colour shapes) is precisely the failure mode this card format exists to avoid.

claim: The triage order when a prompt runs past its token budget — whatever ranks last is what gets dropped. character_first protects the face and wardrobe and will sacrifice the location; style_first defends the look and will happily let a character's hair colour fall off the end.
skip_reason: Only observable when the prompt overflows its token budget and something is discarded. It is an ordering rule applied to the whole prompt rather than content that can be added to it, so on a short card prompt nothing is ever truncated and all four panels render identically. Demonstrating it needs deliberately overlong prompts and a diff of what survived, which is a different experiment.

claim: Sets the TTS voice pool, the caption font and the language of any text drawn inside the frame, all from one word. It is the difference between a stadium whose banners read as a Japanese broadcast and one that reads as a European league tie.

options.clause: english text, banner, sign
japanese text, banner, sign
chinese text, banner, sign
korean text, banner, sign
spanish text, banner, sign
french text, banner, sign
german text, banner, sign

review.issue: Four of the eight options collapse. "spanish text", "french text", "german text" are not danbooru tags at all — the trained tags are english/japanese/korean/chinese/russian text — so es, fr, de and en will all render the same Latin-script gibberish on a banner. Worse, this card contradicts render.watermark, whose skip_reason argues that prompting "english text" only demonstrates SDXL's garbled-lettering failure mode. Both cards cannot be right. Separately, "other" carries an empty clause on a renderable:true card with no note explaining why.
review.fix: Keep only the script-distinct values that have real tags (en, ja, zh, ko) and mark es/fr/de as sharing the Latin-script panel, or mark the whole variable renderable:false reusing the watermark argument and demo the caption font via an ffmpeg overlay. Add a sentence to the claim explaining that "other" is an author passthrough with no canonical panel, the way layer.fg.content does for `custom`.

claim: A permission gate rather than a look: it auto-populates the negative prompt and decides which violence, gore and nudity tags are allowed to pass. These panels show the ceiling of each level — g is the bare subject sentence with nothing gated added, and r is where visible blood becomes legal.

options.clause: sweat, dirty face
bruise, torn clothes, scar
blood, blood on face, injury, bleeding

claim: Decides whether the depth planes are only described inside one prompt or actually rendered and composited as separate images. A director reaches for generated_separate when a foreground element has to move independently of the character, and stays on tag_hinted when they just want a flat generation to imply depth for free.
skip_reason: This is a pipeline/compositing setting, not image content. It governs how the frame is produced (one bake, tag hints, mask-driven, or separate generations composited), not what appears in it — all four options can legitimately produce the identical still, so the panels would be indistinguishable and the card would teach nothing. Demonstrate it with a layer-breakdown diagram or a moving clip, not a still.

claim: Sets how finished the background painting is, which is the contrast lever against character line quality — a sketch background throws every eye onto the face, an ultra_detailed one makes the character a visitor in someone else's world. Reach for it when a frame reads as either empty or too busy to parse.

options.clause: sketch background, rough lineart background, unfinished background
simple background, plain background, minimal background detail
detailed background, scenery
extremely detailed background, intricate scenery, amazing background
painted background, painterly scenery, visible brushstrokes
photorealistic background, photographic scenery, realistic background texture

review.issue: The photobash clause ("photorealistic background, photographic scenery, realistic background texture") smuggles in a global style. In Animagine, `photorealistic` and `realistic` are not plane-scoped — they drag the character off the anime model too, so the panel demonstrates a whole-image style shift rather than a background treatment, which is the "do not smuggle in extra style" rule.
review.fix: Trim to "photorealistic background, realistic scenery" and note in the claim that this value is the one option that bleeds onto the character in SDXL — or reproduce it honestly with a composited photographic plate rather than a clause.

claim: Controls whether the background plane sits darker, level with, or brighter than the subject — the tonal separation that makes a figure pop or dissolve at a glance. Directors pull it darker to lift a character off a busy scene, and go to silhouette when they want shape instead of face.

options.clause: dark background, dimly lit background, background in shadow
even lighting, background and subject same brightness
bright background, brightly lit background, high key background
washed out background, faded background, low contrast background, hazy
silhouetted background, flat dark background shapes, backlit background

review.issue: The `matched` clause contains a prose fragment rather than tags: "background and subject same brightness". Animagine will not parse a comparative relation between two nouns; it will pick up the words `background`, `subject` and `brightness` separately.
review.fix: Use "even lighting, flat lighting, no lighting contrast" — three tags that say the same thing in vocabulary the model has.

claim: States how the background plane travels during a clip: held, drifting, parallaxing at two speeds, or scrolling sideways under a locked character. This is the engine of the anime pan — the character holds a pose while the painting moves behind them.
skip_reason: Purely inter-frame motion of the background plane. In one still, static, drift and parallax_slow are the same image, and scroll_l versus scroll_r cannot be distinguished at all — direction only exists across frames. Any clause would have to fake it with motion blur, which belongs to shot.cam and shot.fx, not this variable. Demo with a 2-second LTX clip instead.

claim: Names the object that sits between the lens and the character, which is the cheapest way to make a flat SDXL generation read as three-dimensional. Reach for it when a frame looks like a poster instead of a photograph — foliage and railings buy depth, glass and doorframes buy confinement. Note that `custom` is an author-supplied tag passthrough with no fixed appearance, so it gets no canonical panel.

options.clause: foliage in foreground, leaves in foreground, blurry foreground
foreground railing, metal railing across frame, blurry foreground
blurry foreground heads, silhouetted spectators in foreground
shot through window, glass in foreground, reflection on glass
curtain in foreground, hanging fabric across frame, blurry foreground
view through doorway, doorframe in foreground, dark frame edges
rain in foreground, raindrops close to lens, blurry foreground droplets
dust motes in foreground, floating particles near lens, foreground bokeh
over the shoulder, out of focus shoulder in foreground, blurry foreground
hand in foreground, out of focus hand near lens, blurry foreground

review.issue: Two clauses fight the fixed sentence. "crowd" restates a tag the subject sentence already contains ("crowd"), so it is the panel most likely to come back reading as the `none` baseline. "shoulder" opens with "over the shoulder", which is a shot-framing tag that implies a second body and collides with "solo" — it also belongs to shot.frame, not this variable.
review.fix: For crowd, push the clause entirely into the near plane and drop the word the subject already owns: "out of focus heads at bottom of frame, silhouetted heads close to lens, blurry foreground". For shoulder, cut "over the shoulder" and keep "out of focus shoulder in foreground, blurry foreground".

claim: Says how the foreground occluder behaves across the clip — held still, swaying, drifting, parallaxing, or passing clean through the lens. Something crossing in front of camera is the single strongest depth cue available in a generated shot.
skip_reason: Same problem one plane forward: this is behaviour over time, not content. A still cannot separate a held branch from a swaying one, and pass_through is defined entirely by the element entering and leaving frame. The only thing a clause could render is smeared motion blur, which is a different variable. Belongs in a clip demo.

claim: Says which depth plane the subject stands on, which decides how large they read, what is allowed to occlude them, and whether defocus lands on them or behind them. Push a character to bg and they become a detail inside a place; pull them to fg and the place becomes their backdrop.

options.clause: subject close to camera, foreground plane, background far behind
subject at middle distance, midground plane, background behind subject
distant subject, small figure in the distance, far background plane
subject just ahead of midground, near foreground plane, slight foreground overlap

review.issue: "between_fg_mid" is written as descriptive prose fragments with no tag the model knows — "subject just ahead of midground", "near foreground plane", "slight foreground overlap" — and semantically it sits inside the gap between fg and mid, so it will land on top of one of them. The fg/mid/bg clauses are also non-tag phrasings ("subject at middle distance", "midground plane") that rely on the text encoder parsing English relations.
review.fix: Rewrite on tags the model responds to: fg = "close-up, subject near camera, blurry background, depth of field"; mid = "cowboy shot, subject at middle distance, background in focus"; bg = "wide shot, tiny figure, distant subject". Drop between_fg_mid or give it a concrete occlusion cue ("partially occluded by foreground object") so it has something of its own to render.

claim: States how bodies travel relative to each other — the difference between two people converging on a confrontation and two people drifting past without ever meeting. A director reaches for it to give a scene geometry that means something before anyone speaks.

options.clause: 2boys, standing, facing viewer
2boys, walking toward each other, facing each other
2boys, walking away, backs turned, from behind
2boys, circling each other, facing each other, wide stance
2boys, side-by-side, walking, same direction
2boys, facing each other, standoff, confrontation
2boys, passing each other, opposite directions, walking
2boys, crossing paths, walking, different directions
multiple boys, converging, gathering into a huddle
multiple boys, scattering, running in different directions
2boys, single file, one following behind the other, walking

review.issue: Most of the options are trajectories, and a still only shows the instantaneous arrangement. approach / face_off / circle all reduce to "two boys facing each other"; pass_by / cross both reduce to "two boys walking in different directions"; retreat / follow both come back as two backs walking away. That is the same argument the card set already accepts for layer.fg.motion and block.entrance's reveal_by_pan — applied inconsistently here.
review.fix: Either mark the variable renderable:false with a motion skip_reason, or keep only the values with a distinct frozen geometry (static, face_off, side_by_side, follow, gather, scatter) and demote approach/retreat/circle/pass_by/cross to a clip demo with a note in the claim.

claim: How a character arrives in the frame. Entering from an edge makes the audience wait and turns the arrival into an event; already_present makes the character part of the place instead of a visitor to it.

review.issue: Two problems. "none" (empty clause) and "already_present" ("standing, centered in frame, fully visible") produce the same image — the bare subject sentence already renders a standing, centred, fully visible boy — so two panels are duplicates. And "reveal_by_pan" has an empty clause on a renderable:true card with no explanation anywhere in the claim, so it reads as an authoring omission rather than an honest zero.
review.fix: Drop "none" and let already_present be the baseline (or vice versa, with a note that none == already_present in a still). Add a clause to the claim: reveal_by_pan is camera motion across frames and gets no panel.

claim: Controls how this shot arrives on screen — snapped in hard on a cut, bled up out of black, or thrown in on a whip pan — and it lives on the shot that owns the change rather than on some seam between shots. A director reaches for it to set how much ceremony an entrance gets: a smash into a face and a slow dissolve into a memory are the same field, one word apart.
skip_reason: A transition is an event between two shots, and a still has no outgoing shot to arrive from — the variable's entire content is what happens across the boundary. The options with a visible mid-transition frame degrade into unrelated lessons: fade_black renders as a dim scene, fade_white and flash as a blown-out one, dissolve as a double exposure, whip_pan as motion blur, so the panel would teach exposure and blur rather than arrival. Worse, cut, smash and match_cut have no single-frame signature whatsoever, so three panels would come back byte-identical to the base subject and the grid would read as a broken render rather than an honest zero.

claim: Controls how this shot leaves, which is what lets a scene's final shot fade on its own instead of requiring a phantom shot after it just to hold the black. The option that justifies its separate existence is hold: a shot that refuses to end is a different beat from one that cuts, and only an outgoing field can say so.
skip_reason: Departure is defined purely by what the shot does after its last authored frame, and a still is that frame with nothing following it — hold and cut produce literally the same image, which is the proof that the axis is temporal. The visually-distinct options (fade_black, fade_white, flash, dissolve, whip_pan) would only render as darkness, blowout, blend or blur, none of which an author would read as 'this is how the shot exits'; they would read as grade and lens choices already covered by other namespaces.

claim: Gives a direction to the transitions that are meaningless without one — a wipe, an iris and a whip pan all have to travel somewhere, and left versus right decides whether the cut agrees with the character's screen direction or fights it. Set it wrong and a chase reverses itself at every boundary.
skip_reason: This is a modifier on a moving mask, not on the image: it changes where a wipe edge or iris boundary is travelling, and a still frame has no travel. It is also doubly dependent — direction only means anything once the parent transition is a wipe, iris or whip pan, and those are themselves unrenderable here, so a panel grid would be a modifier on nothing. The mask itself is a compositing overlay applied after generation and has no danbooru tag that would put it in the frame.

claim: Punctuates the boundary between scenes, and it defaults harder than a shot boundary does (fade_black rather than cut) because an audience needs to feel a location or time change, not just register it. Reach for match_cut when the two scenes rhyme and for smash when you want the change to hurt.
skip_reason: Scene punctuation is an event spanning two scenes; its meaning is the relationship between the outgoing and incoming images, which no single frame contains. match_cut is the clearest case — it is defined entirely by shape agreement with a frame that does not exist in this panel — and time_card replaces the subject with a text card, which would violate the fixed-subject method outright and which Animagine renders as garbled glyphs anyway.

claim: Marks structural breaks between chapters, where the audience should feel the film take a breath — long_dissolve for time collapsing, title_card for a formal new movement, cut only when you want the chapter break to sneak past unannounced. It is deliberately a shorter menu than the scene-level one because chapter breaks should be few and unmistakable.
skip_reason: Like the other transition fields this is a boundary event with no single-frame existence, and the two options that come closest to being images are the worst fit for this method: title_card is a full-frame graphic that replaces the subject sentence entirely, and long_dissolve differs from dissolve only in duration, which is by definition invisible in a still. A grid here would show one dark panel, one bright panel and four panels indistinguishable from the base.

claim: Declares that a scene is a montage and which kind, which changes its whole shape — shot lengths, cut rate, whether music carries it and whether dialogue is allowed at all. An author reaches for it to compress weeks of training or a journey into twenty seconds without hand-authoring every fragment.
skip_reason: A montage is a multi-shot form whose entire meaning lives in accumulation and cutting rhythm; one still is one fragment of it and cannot show that fragments repeat, escalate or span time. The option names are also content descriptions rather than looks, so any clause that tried to render them (sweat and exhaustion for training, luggage and platforms for travel) would rewrite what the subject is doing and where he is, breaking the rule that the subject sentence is identical in every panel and that the clause expresses only the option.

claim: Decides what gives when your authored shot durations don't add up to the scene length the structure asked for: free lets the scene run long, fit_to_budget and stretch_to_budget rescale every shot to hit the number, trim_tail amputates the end, and drop_lowest_priority sacrifices whole filler shots to protect the hero ones. A director reaches for it when a locked runtime — an OP, a music video, a broadcast slot — has to be hit without hand-retiming forty shots.
skip_reason: Pure duration arithmetic across a timeline. It changes how long shots play and which shots survive to the cut, never what is inside any single frame. All five options would render a byte-identical still.

claim: The one inheritable tempo word: it sets default shot length and cut rate for everything beneath it, so languid holds a frame until the viewer notices the silence while frantic cuts away before the eye has finished reading. Directors set it once per sequence instead of typing durations into every shot.
skip_reason: Pace exists only as duration and cut rate measured across a sequence; a single frame has no length. Any tag that faked it — motion blur, speed lines, an action pose — would be demonstrating a different variable and rewriting the subject's body, which the fixed subject sentence forbids.

claim: The pattern of shot lengths rather than their average: even is metronomic and safe, accelerating tightens the screw toward a climax, decelerating lets a scene settle, long_short is the classic setup-then-punchline pair, and breathing swells and relaxes like a chest. This is what separates an edit that feels composed from one that feels merely uniform.
skip_reason: Rhythm is a relationship between consecutive shot durations and does not exist until there are several shots in a row. A still has no duration and no neighbours, so all seven options collapse to the same image.

claim: Time manipulation inside a single shot: ramp_down drops into slow motion for the emotional beat, slowmo_hit stretches the frame of impact then snaps back to speed, freeze_then_go pins a pose before releasing it, and stutter chops playback into judder. This is core anime action grammar and the main reason a fight reads as choreography instead of generic movement.
skip_reason: Every option is a change in playback speed over time, so the distinction lives strictly between frames. A still cannot tell ramp_up from ramp_down, and tagging 'motion blur' to suggest slow motion would show off the blur variable, not the ramp.

claim: Whether cuts may land anywhere or must snap to the generated music: music_beat for tight percussive cutting, music_bar and music_phrase for cuts that breathe with the song's structure, metronome for a fixed pulse independent of any track. Switch it off free and a montage floats against its own score; switch it on and the edit suddenly feels scored rather than soundtracked.
skip_reason: A quantisation rule between the edit and an audio track. It moves cut points in time and is defined by sound the still cannot contain; nothing about it survives into a single frame.

review.issue: cool_film ("cool colors, blue tint, cold color palette") and night_blue ("blue theme, deep blue shadows, cool tint") are the same instruction to the model expressed twice; with a floodlit night stadium as the fixed subject both will also sit close to the ungraded baseline, so the pair reads as a render glitch rather than two looks.
review.fix: Give night_blue a value component the other lacks — "blue theme, night, dark, deep blue shadows" — so one panel is a hue shift and the other is a hue shift plus a darkening, or fold the two values together.

claim: Controls how tone is distributed rather than what colour it is: where black sits, how hard the midtones climb, whether highlights clip. Crushed makes a frame airless and expensive, lifted_matte makes it feel like recovered footage, and linear is the flat ungraded read that tells the audience nothing has been decided yet.

options.clause: flat contrast, even tonal range, even tones
cinematic contrast, deep blacks, bright highlights

review.issue: strong_s ("high contrast, crushed blacks, blown highlights") and crushed ("crushed blacks, pure black shadows, very high contrast") share both load-bearing tags — crushed blacks plus very high contrast. The two panels will be the same image with a different label, which is exactly the case where a card teaches nothing.
review.fix: Let crushed own the black point alone ("crushed blacks, pure black shadows") and rewrite strong_s around the S-curve's highlight end ("high contrast, blown highlights, bright specular highlights"), so one panel is about shadows and the other about highlights.

claim: Moves the grade across the duration of a single shot so a mood can turn without a cut: the frame warms as a memory lands, or drains to desaturated as hope leaves the character. A director reaches for it when the change belongs to the person, not to the edit.
skip_reason: This is a transition over time, not a look. Any single frame shows only one point on the ramp, so a still cannot distinguish to_warm from an already-warm preset, and cannot distinguish none from any of the moving options at all. It needs a two-frame or clip comparison, not a capability still.

claim: Decides which pixels the grade is allowed to touch. Grading full_frame is exactly what drags a locked character colour off-model; exclude_characters lets the world go cold while the cast stays on their approved palette, and shadows_only or highlights_only let you tint the darkness without bleaching skin. Note the carrier tint is held constant across these panels so only the masked region varies.

options.clause: desaturated blue tint, entire image tinted, uniform color cast
spot color, desaturated blue background, character in natural color
blue tinted shadows, cool shadow tint, neutral highlights
blue tinted highlights, cool highlight tint, neutral shadows
selective color, red hues shifted, remaining colors desaturated

review.issue: shadows_only and highlights_only are written in invented vocabulary ("blue tinted shadows", "cool highlight tint", "neutral highlights") that has no danbooru anchor. SDXL has no tonal-mask concept, so both will read as a globally blue frame — i.e. indistinguishable from each other and from full_frame, making three of five panels the same. This is the same class of failure the render.watermark card correctly refuses: a post-generation mask being faked with tags.
review.fix: Keep the three values the model can actually express — full_frame, exclude_characters ("spot color" is a real, reliable tag) and hue_range ("selective color" likewise) — and demonstrate shadows_only/highlights_only as ffmpeg-masked grades over one identical render, exactly as the watermark card proposes.
